title: Hello, Me!
summary: Babies learn who they are through the faces, voices and names of the people who care for them. This unit fills the day with mirrors, family photos, name songs and warm face-to-face moments so each baby feels known and at home in the room.
big_questions: How does each baby show us they recognize a familiar face or voice?
What do babies do when they see themselves in a mirror?
How can family photos help a baby feel safe and connected during the day?

goals.text: Babies feel a sense of belonging when they see their families and hear their names in the room.
Babies explore faces, including their own, by looking, smiling, touching and copying.
Babies use sounds, smiles and gestures to start and keep a back-and-forth exchange.
Babies build strength and body awareness while lifting their heads, reaching and crawling toward faces and photos.
Babies feel calm and secure through predictable greetings and responsive comfort.

activities.title: Peekaboo Mirror
materials: Unbreakable acrylic mirror, secured at floor level
steps: Sit with the baby in front of the mirror so you can both be seen.
Say the baby's name and point to their reflection. Pause and watch their face.
Cover the mirror with the blanket, then lift it: “Peekaboo, there you are!”
Follow the baby's lead. If they look away, rest and try again later.
activities.safety: Use only shatterproof mirrors with no loose frame parts; check edges daily.

activities.title: Family Photo Book
materials: Family photos in a soft fabric photo book or sturdy clear-sleeve board album
steps: Settle with one or two babies and open the book to their family's page.
Name who you see: “That's your grandma. She waved goodbye this morning.”
Wait for a look, a point or a sound, then answer it warmly.
Leave the book in a low basket so babies can return to it on their own.
activities.safety: Keep photos sealed in the book; no loose laminated cards with sharp corners.

activities.title: Hello Name Song
materials: A simple hello song you make up with each child's name
steps: Gather babies who are interested; never require everyone to join.
Sing hello to each baby by name and make eye contact as you sing.
Wave, then pause. Celebrate any wave, kick, smile or sound in return.
Keep it short, two or three minutes, and end before interest fades.

activities.title: Tummy-Time Mirror
steps: Place the baby on their tummy on the mat, facing the mirror.
Get down at eye level and talk about the face they see.
Watch for tired signs, like fussing or a dropped head, and roll them over to rest.
Try a few short sessions through the day rather than one long one.
activities.safety: Tummy time only while the baby is awake and an educator is right beside them.

activities.title: Face-to-Face Chats
materials: A comfortable spot to sit close
steps: Hold the baby about 20–30 cm from your face, where they can see you best.
Make a slow, simple expression: a big smile, an open mouth, raised eyebrows.
Wait. Give the baby time to copy or respond, then copy them back.
Name what you notice: “You stuck out your tongue too!”

activities.title: Where Is Your Nose?
materials: Large soft doll with sewn-on features
steps: Touch your own nose and say “nose” slowly and clearly.
Gently touch the baby's nose, or the doll's, and say it again.
Ask “Where is your nose?” and wait. Celebrate any look or reach.
Add one new body part at a time over the two weeks.
activities.safety: Dolls must have embroidered features only, with nothing glued or sewn on that could come loose.

activities.title: Hello Neighbourhood Walk
steps: Take a slow walk around the yard or block.
Say hello to what you pass: “Hello, tree! Hello, dog!” and wave.
Point out people and pause so babies can look and listen.
Talk about where their families might be: “Mama is at work. She'll come back after nap.”
activities.safety: Keep babies under 6 months out of direct sun; dress for the weather and check straps before leaving.

activities.title: Photo Wall Crawl
materials: Family photos sealed under clear contact paper at baby height
Firm play mat along the wall
steps: Place photos low on the wall where crawlers and sitters can see and pat them.
Encourage a baby to move toward their photo: “Who's that? Let's go see Papa!”
Sit beside them and name the people they touch.
Notice which photos each baby seeks out and share that with families.
activities.safety: Check daily that contact paper is fully sealed with no peeling edges a baby could pull off and mouth.

activities.title: Scarf Peekaboo
steps: Drape the scarf over the toy while the baby watches.
Ask “Where did it go?” and wait for the baby to look or reach.
Lift the scarf together: “There it is!”
Try covering your own face next, and let the baby pull the scarf away.
activities.safety: Use scarves only with an educator present; put them away after play and never leave one near a sleeping baby.

schedule.focus: Faces and names: mirrors, smiles and hearing our names sung
My people: family photos, body parts and moving toward the faces we love

observe: How does each baby respond when they hear their name: a turn of the head, a smile, stillness?
Which babies look longer at their own reflection, and what do they do next?
Who reaches for or pats a family photo, and which person do they seek out?
How long can a baby keep a back-and-forth exchange going before needing a break?
What cues tell you a baby is tired or overwhelmed, and how do they calm?
Does the baby search for a toy hidden under the scarf? What strategies do they try?
family: Invite each family to send 3–5 photos of the people, pets and places that matter to their baby.
Ask families how they say “hello”, “mama”, “papa” or other family names in their home language, and use those words.
Share a short note or photo when a baby smiles at their family's picture during the day.
Suggest a mirror game at home: sit together in front of a mirror and name what you see.
Ask families which songs or rhymes they sing at home so you can sing them here too.
inclusion: For babies with low vision, use high-contrast photos and bring faces closer; pair every greeting with touch and voice.
For babies who are hard of hearing, face them when you speak, use gestures and simple signs, and keep background noise low.
Offer supported sitting (a U-shaped cushion or your lap) for babies who are not yet stable on the floor.
Some babies find long eye contact intense; follow their cues and let them glance away and come back.
Make sure the photo wall reflects every family structure in the room; ask families how they would like to be represented.
Talk with families and any resource consultant about the comfort strategies that work best for their baby.

tips: Sing the hello song in French too: “Bonjour, Sami, bonjour!”
Label the photo wall with “Ma famille” and each family's own word for family.
Ask families for names they use at home, like grandparent names, and use them exactly.
Respond to every sound or gesture as communication, whatever the language.

safety_notes: Mirrors must be shatterproof and secured; check them and all photo displays daily for loose or peeling parts.
Nothing used in this unit should fit through a choke-tube tester; dolls and soft toys need sewn-on features only.
Play scarves are used only with an educator present and are stored out of reach afterward.

title: Touch and Feel
summary: Babies learn about the world through their hands, feet and mouths. This unit offers safe, large textures, sealed sensory bottles and supervised water so babies can explore soft, bumpy, smooth, warm and cool while an educator names what they feel.
big_questions: Which textures does each baby seek out, and which ones do they avoid?
How do babies use their hands, feet and mouths to find out about new things?
How do our words help a baby make sense of what they feel?

goals.text: Babies explore a range of safe textures with hands, feet and bodies.
Babies show what they like and dislike through faces, sounds and movement, and educators respond.
Babies hear simple describing words (soft, bumpy, wet, cool) during play.
Babies notice that their actions cause things to happen, like splashes and swirling bottles.
Babies feel safe to try new sensations with a trusted educator close by.

activities.title: Texture Wall Crawl
materials: Large texture panels fixed to a low wall: carpet square, rubber mat, corduroy, faux fur
steps: Mount the panels low, where crawlers and sitters can reach.
Sit by the wall and stroke one panel yourself: “Ooh, this one is fuzzy.”
Wait for the baby to reach or crawl over, then name what they touch.
Notice which panel they return to and mention it at pick-up.
activities.safety: Screw or firmly fix every panel; check daily for loose threads, peeling glue or frayed edges.

activities.title: Fabric Treasure Basket
materials: Large hemmed fabric squares: velvet, satin, fleece, denim, terry cloth
steps: Set the basket beside a sitting baby and sit close without directing.
Watch what they pull out first, and how: grab, rub, wave, mouth.
Name the fabric in a calm voice: “Smooth. That's shiny satin.”
Let the baby lead; your job is to notice and add a word or two.
activities.safety: Hem all edges, trim loose threads, and wash fabrics after mouthing.

activities.title: Swirly Sensory Bottles
materials: Water, baby oil and a drop of food colouring inside
Strong glue and tape for the lids
steps: Lay a bottle on its side near a baby on their tummy or sitting.
Roll it slowly and wonder aloud: “Look, the colours are moving!”
Pause and let the baby roll, shake or push it.
Notice whether they track the movement or look to you to share it.
activities.safety: Glue AND tape every lid before use; check bottles daily and remove any that crack or leak.

activities.title: Warm and Cool Cloths
materials: Warm (not hot) and cool water in basins out of reach
steps: Test the warm cloth on your inner wrist first; it should feel just comfortably warm.
Gently touch the cloth to the baby's hand or foot: “This one is warm.”
Try the cool cloth and watch their face. Name what you see.
Stop if the baby turns away or fusses; offer a cuddle instead.
activities.safety: Keep water basins out of babies' reach, with an educator within arm's reach; tip out water when done.

activities.title: Splash Tray
materials: Shallow tray with 2–3 cm of lukewarm water
Large cups and a big sponge
steps: Seat one or two sitting babies at the tray with you right beside them.
Pat the water and say “splash!” then wait to see if the baby copies.
Offer a cup or sponge and narrate: “Squeeze. Drip, drip, drip.”
Tip out the water as soon as play ends and dry hands together.
activities.safety: An educator stays within arm's reach the whole time; babies can drown in very shallow water. Tip out water immediately after.

activities.title: Grass Under Our Feet
materials: Large blanket in a shaded spot
steps: Check the grass first for litter, sticks, droppings, mushrooms and stones, and remove them.
Sit on the blanket with a baby in your lap and let their bare feet brush the grass.
Name the feeling: “Tickly grass! Cool grass!”
Follow their cues: some will dig in, some will pull back. Both are fine.
activities.safety: Shade for babies under 6 months; watch closely for mouthing and never let babies eat anything found outside.

activities.title: Touch-and-Feel Book Snuggle
materials: Touch-and-feel board books with fixed textures
steps: Hold the baby on your lap with the book in front of you both.
Guide your own finger over a texture and describe it.
Pause and let the baby pat or scratch the page.
Read the same book again tomorrow; repetition builds understanding.
activities.safety: Remove books with peeling or loose texture patches.

activities.title: Bumpy Ball Roll
materials: Large soft textured sensory balls, bigger than a choke-tube opening
steps: Roll a ball gently toward a sitting or crawling baby.
Describe the bumps as they grab it: “Bumpy, bumpy ball.”
Hold out your hands and wait to see if they push it back.
Cheer any movement toward or with the ball.
activities.safety: Check balls for tears or nubs that could come off.

activities.title: Texture Tunnel
materials: Large sturdy box with both ends open, edges taped smooth
Fabric and bath-mat pieces glued firmly inside
steps: Lay the tunnel on the mat and peek at the baby through the other end.
Call their name and wait for them to crawl toward you.
Talk about the textures under their hands as they move.
Let non-crawlers lie half in and pat the floor of the tunnel.
activities.safety: Keep both ends open so you can always see the baby; check glued pieces daily.

schedule.focus: Soft, smooth and fuzzy: first textures with hands and feet
Wet, cool and bumpy: water, moving bottles and crawling over textures

observe: Which textures does each baby reach for first, and which do they pull away from?
How does the baby explore: patting, rubbing, squeezing, mouthing, kicking?
Does the baby look to you before or after touching something new?
What happens when the baby splashes or rolls the bottle? Do they try it again on purpose?
How does the baby show they have had enough, and how quickly do they settle?
Which describing words seem to catch the baby's attention?
family: Ask families to send a clean scrap of fabric from home (an old shirt or blanket corner) for the treasure basket.
Share a photo of the baby exploring a texture they loved.
Suggest bare-feet time at home on different floors: a rug, a towel, grass.
Ask families which textures their baby enjoys or dislikes at home, including at bath time.
Learn how families say “soft”, “wet” and “warm” in their home language and use those words.
inclusion: Some babies are sensitive to touch; offer textures near them and let them choose, rather than placing items on their skin.
For babies who seek strong sensory input, offer firmer textures and deep, gentle pressure like a bear hug, if the family is comfortable with it.
For babies with limited hand movement, bring textures to the feet, cheeks or forearms, and tilt trays within reach.
Offer supported seating so every baby can reach the splash tray and basket at a comfortable height.
For babies with low vision, choose high-contrast fabrics and narrate every new texture before it touches them.
Talk with families and any resource consultant about sensory preferences and helpful strategies.

tips: Pair each describing word in English and French: “Soft, doux.”
Label the texture wall panels in both languages.
Invite families to share words for textures in their home language.
Accept any sound, gesture or word as the baby's answer.

safety_notes: Every material must be larger than a choke-tube opening; sensory bottles have lids glued AND taped and are checked daily.
Water play only with an educator within arm's reach; tip out water as soon as play ends.
No food is used as a play material in this unit. If you add a taste, use only foods each family has already introduced at home, and check every child's allergy and dietary list first.
Wash fabrics and wipe toys after mouthing to reduce the spread of germs.

title: Sounds and Songs
summary: Voices, rhythm and simple instruments are some of a baby's first joys. This unit fills the room with songs, lap bounces, copycat sounds and safe things to bang and shake, building connection, listening and early language.
big_questions: Which sounds and songs make each baby light up, and which calm them?
How do babies use their voices and bodies to join in with music?
What happens when we copy a baby's sounds back to them?

goals.text: Babies enjoy songs and rhymes with familiar adults and feel connected through shared music.
Babies make sounds with their voices and with safe instruments, and notice the sounds they cause.
Babies listen to and turn toward voices and sounds around them.
Babies move their bodies to rhythm: bouncing, swaying, kicking and clapping.
Babies hear songs from their own homes and cultures in the room.

activities.title: Lap Bounce Rhymes
materials: A few short bouncing rhymes you know well
steps: Sit the baby on your lap facing you, with their head and trunk well supported.
Chant a rhyme with a gentle bounce on the beat.
Pause before the last line and wait. Does the baby wiggle or look for more?
Keep bounces gentle; slow down or stop if the baby looks unsure.
activities.safety: Bounce gently and support the head; no tossing or jerky movements.

activities.title: Pots and Spoons Band
materials: Large plastic bowls turned upside down
steps: Set pots and bowls on the floor near sitting babies.
Tap one yourself, then hand a spoon to a baby and wait.
Name the sound they make: “Bang! Loud!” or “Tap, tap, quiet.”
Copy their rhythm back to them and see if they notice.
activities.safety: Use wooden spoons with smooth, uncracked handles; watch for babies poking near faces.

activities.title: Sealed Shaker Bottles
materials: Clear sturdy bottles holding large plastic lids from the recycling
Strong glue and tape for the lids
steps: Shake a bottle near the baby, then hold it still and wait.
Offer the bottle and watch what they do with it.
Shake fast and slow and name it: “Fast, fast! Slooow.”
Sing a familiar song while shaking together.
activities.safety: Glue AND tape every lid; check daily and remove any bottle that cracks. Rattles must be labelled for under-3s.

activities.title: Everybody's Name Song
steps: Invite interested babies to gather; others can listen from where they play.
Sing each baby's name into the tune and wave.
Add a clap or pat on the floor for the rhythm of their name.
Wait for a smile, sound or wave before moving to the next name.

activities.title: Copycat Coos
steps: Get face to face with the baby and wait for them to make a sound.
Copy the sound back, matching their pitch and length.
Pause again. Give the baby a turn.
Once a pattern starts, try a slightly new sound and see if they copy you.

activities.title: Sway and Dance
materials: Calm and lively music at a low volume
steps: Hold a baby securely and sway slowly to calm music.
Switch to a faster song and step side to side.
Invite floor-sitters to bounce and crawlers to move with you.
Notice which tempo each baby prefers and return to it.
activities.safety: Keep the volume low; babies' ears are sensitive. Keep any music player and cords out of reach.

activities.title: Outdoor Sound Hunt
materials: Stroller or blanket in the shade
steps: Settle outside and stay quiet for a moment.
When a sound happens, cup your ear and name it: “A bird! Tweet, tweet.”
Watch where the baby turns and follow their gaze.
Copy the sound and invite the baby to try.
activities.safety: Shade for babies under 6 months; dress for the weather and check for anything babies could put in their mouths.

activities.title: Drum Fast, Drum Slow
materials: Hand drum or sturdy upturned bin
Soft-headed beater sized for small hands
steps: Pat the drum slowly, then quickly, and say what you're doing.
Offer the baby a turn with their hands or the beater.
When they hit it, respond with a matching pat.
Stop and start the beat; see if the baby stops and starts too.
activities.safety: Beaters must be one piece with no detachable head.

activities.title: Quiet Song Cuddle
materials: A gentle song from a family's home
steps: Hold a baby who wants closeness and hum or sing softly.
Match your breathing and pace to a slow, steady rhythm.
Watch for the baby's body to soften and their gaze to settle.
Let the baby decide when to return to play.

activities.title: Floating Scarf Dance
steps: Wave a scarf high and low to the music while babies watch.
Let it float down near a baby and wait for them to grab.
Invite crawlers to chase a scarf you drag slowly along the floor.
Name the movement: “Up, up, up… and down!”
activities.safety: Use scarves only with an educator present; put them away after play.

schedule.focus: Voices first: names, copycat sounds, rhymes and listening outside
Making music: banging, shaking, drumming and dancing to the beat

observe: Which songs or sounds make each baby kick, smile or go still?
How long does a copycat exchange last before the baby looks away?
Does the baby repeat an action, like banging, to make the sound happen again?
Which babies turn toward a sound they cannot see?
How does each baby respond to loud versus quiet sounds?
Which songs from home seem to comfort a baby the most?
family: Ask each family for a song, lullaby or rhyme they sing at home, in any language, and learn it.
Make a simple song list with the words for families to sing at home.
Suggest a kitchen band at home: a pot, a wooden spoon and a lot of fun.
Share a short note about a sound the baby copied today.
Invite a family member to drop in and sing or play an instrument with the group.
inclusion: For babies who are hard of hearing, let them feel vibrations: a hand on the drum or on your chest while you sing.
For babies sensitive to noise, offer a quieter corner and softer sounds, and keep loud play short.
Offer instruments with large, easy grips and place them where babies with limited movement can reach.
Use simple signs or gestures with songs, like “more” and “all done”, so every baby can join in.
Talk with families and any resource consultant about which sounds soothe or overwhelm their baby.

tips: Sing familiar French songs and rhymes alongside English ones.
Use “encore” with a gesture when a baby asks for more of a song.
Collect songs in every home language in the room and rotate them.
Respond to every babble as a turn in the conversation, in any language.

safety_notes: Shaker bottles have lids glued AND taped and hold only large items; check them every day.
Instruments must have no small detachable parts; rattles are labelled for under-3s.
Keep music players and their cords up high, out of babies' reach; keep volume low.
Scarves are used only with an educator present and are stored away after play.

title: Moving and Grooving
summary: In their first year and a half, babies go from lifting their heads to rolling, crawling, cruising and taking first steps. This unit gives every baby safe floor time and inviting challenges at their own stage, with an educator nearby to cheer, wait and support.
big_questions: What is each baby working on right now, and how can we set up the space to support it?
How do babies solve movement problems, like getting to a toy just out of reach?
How does a familiar adult nearby give babies the courage to try?

goals.text: Babies build strength and control through daily tummy time, rolling, crawling and cruising.
Babies reach, grasp and let go of objects with growing control.
Babies keep trying when movement is hard and find their own ways to get where they want to go.
Babies share the joy of moving with educators and other babies.
Babies use their bodies to communicate: kicking with excitement, reaching to be picked up, waving.

activities.title: Tummy-Time Treasures
materials: High-contrast cloth book or large soft toy
steps: Place the baby on their tummy and lie down facing them.
Stand the book or toy just in front of them at eye level.
Talk softly to encourage head-lifting. Wait; don't rush.
Roll them onto their back at the first sign of tiredness.
activities.safety: Tummy time only while the baby is awake and an educator is right beside them, on a firm surface.

activities.title: Reach and Grab
materials: Soft toys bigger than a choke-tube opening
steps: Hold a toy just within reach of a baby lying on their back or sitting.
Wait for them to reach. Name it: “You're reaching!”
Let them grasp it, then offer a second toy to the other hand.
Notice which hand leads and whether they pass toys between hands.

activities.title: Roll Over, Roll Back
materials: Bright toy to the side of the baby
steps: Lay the baby on their back and place a toy just off to one side.
Call their name from that side so they turn their head.
Wait while they try to roll. Resist helping too soon.
Celebrate the effort, roll or no roll: “You worked so hard!”
activities.safety: Practise on the floor only, with nothing hard nearby and an educator beside the baby.

activities.title: Cushion Mountain Crawl
materials: Firm foam wedges and low foam blocks
steps: Arrange a low, gentle slope of foam shapes on the mats.
Sit at the top and call to the crawler to come and find you.
Spot closely without lifting; let them work out where to put hands and knees.
Name their moves: “Up, up, up! Now down.”
activities.safety: Use firm foam only (no pillows or soft bedding); keep climbs low and stay within arm's reach.

activities.title: Tunnel Peekaboo
materials: Short fabric crawl tunnel or large open box
steps: Lie at one end and peek through at the baby on the other side.
Say “Peekaboo! Come find me!” and wait.
Welcome them with a big smile when they reach you.
Switch ends and let them watch another baby crawl through.
activities.safety: Keep the tunnel short with both ends open so you can always see the baby.

activities.title: Cruising Path
materials: Sturdy low furniture anchored to the wall or floor
Soft toys placed along the top
steps: Line up the furniture so a baby can hold on and step sideways.
Place a toy a little farther along each time.
Stay close and narrate: “Step, step… you got it!”
Let them sit down when they choose; practising getting down safely matters too.
activities.safety: Anchor all furniture; check for tipping, sharp corners and anything babies could pull down.

activities.title: Push-Along Walk
materials: Sturdy weighted push toy or low wooden cart
steps: Help a cruiser pull to stand at the push toy.
Walk backward slowly in front of them, inviting them to follow.
Keep the path clear and talk about where you're going.
Let them rest and try again; short tries are fine.
activities.safety: Use push toys that won't tip; never place walkers near stairs or on slopes.

activities.title: Ball Back-and-Forth
steps: Sit facing a sitting baby with legs apart to make a little play zone.
Roll the ball gently to them and say their name.
Hold out your hands and wait for them to push it back.
Invite a second baby to join the circle when they show interest.

activities.title: Blanket Wiggles Outside
steps: Check the area for litter, sticks and stones before laying the blanket.
Offer tummy time and back time on the blanket under the trees.
Point to what moves above: leaves, clouds, birds.
Encourage kicking and reaching as babies watch the world move.
activities.safety: Shade for babies under 6 months; dress for the weather and watch closely for mouthing.

activities.title: Clap, Kick and Wave Song
materials: A simple action song you make up
steps: Sing a short song with one action per verse: clap, kick, wave.
Do the action slowly so babies can watch and try.
Help a willing baby feel the action by gently moving their hands, if they welcome it.
Repeat the same song daily so babies can anticipate the moves.

activities.title: Grass Crawl Adventure
materials: A checked, shaded patch of grass or smooth path
steps: Check the ground carefully and remove anything small or sharp.
Let crawlers move across the grass and walkers practise on the path.
Name the surface: “Bumpy grass. Smooth path.”
Stay close and follow, letting the baby choose the direction.
activities.safety: Sun protection and shade; never let babies eat anything found outside, and check for mushrooms and droppings first.

activities.title: Drop It In
materials: Large soft blocks or balls bigger than a choke-tube opening
steps: Drop a block into the bin and say “In! Plop!”
Offer the baby a block and wait.
Celebrate when they let go: “You dropped it in!”
Tip the bin over together and start again.

activities.title: Mirror Wiggles
steps: Sit beside the baby in front of the mirror.
Wiggle, wave or kick, then pause to let them watch.
Copy any move they make: “You kicked! I'll kick too!”
Name body parts as they move.
activities.safety: Use only shatterproof, secured mirrors.

schedule.focus: Head up, roll over, reach out: tummy time and first reaching
On the move: crawling over, through and toward
Pulling up and stepping out: cruising, pushing and early walking

observe: What movement is each baby working on right now: lifting, rolling, crawling, pulling up, cruising, stepping?
How does the baby solve getting to a toy that is just out of reach?
How long does the baby keep trying before looking to an adult for help?
Does the baby use both sides of their body, or favour one side?
Who watches other babies move, and do they try to copy them?
How does the baby show excitement or frustration with their body?
family: Share one new movement you saw this week, with a photo if the family has given consent.
Suggest short, frequent tummy time at home on the floor, with a parent lying face to face.
Ask families what movements they see at home that may not show up at the centre.
Share simple action songs so families can sing them at home.
Invite families to send a photo of a favourite place their baby likes to move: a park, a hallway, a rug.
inclusion: Set up the space for each baby's current stage instead of the age chart; every baby gets a reachable challenge.
Use positioning supports, like rolled towels or a U-shaped cushion, as recommended by the family or a therapist.
For babies with limited mobility, bring toys and peers to them and use your words to celebrate every movement.
Ask before guiding a baby's body; use gentle touch only when the baby welcomes it and the family is comfortable.
Keep pathways wide and clear for babies who use mobility equipment.
Talk with families and any resource consultant or therapist about goals and how to support them in play.

tips: Cheer with “Bravo!” and narrate moves in French: “Tu marches!”
Sing the action song in French: “Je tape des mains, je tape des pieds.”
Ask families how they cheer their baby on at home, in their own language.
Use gestures with every movement word so meaning is clear in any language.

safety_notes: Tummy time only while babies are awake and closely supervised, on a firm surface.
Anchor all furniture babies pull up on; check foam pieces, mats and push toys daily for wear.
All toys and balls must be bigger than a choke-tube opening; no cords longer than 15 cm.
Outdoors: shade for babies under 6 months, weather-appropriate clothing, and a ground check before play.

title: Little Nature Explorers
summary: Fall brings crunchy leaves, cool breezes and long shadows. This unit takes babies outside every day and brings safe pieces of the season inside, so they can look, listen, touch and move in nature with an educator close by.
big_questions: What do babies notice when they are outside in the fall?
How do babies respond to changing light, wind and sound?
How can we share the outdoors safely with babies who explore with their mouths?

goals.text: Babies spend time outdoors every day and grow comfortable in fresh air.
Babies explore leaves, light and shadow with their senses and with a trusted adult.
Babies hear words for what they see and feel outdoors, and use sounds and gestures to share.
Babies move their bodies on different outdoor surfaces: grass, leaves, paths.
Babies notice movement and change, like falling leaves and moving shadows.

activities.title: Leaf Window
steps: Seal the leaves between two sheets of contact paper and tape them to a low window.
Bring a baby close and watch the light shine through.
Pat a leaf and name its colour: “Red leaf. Yellow leaf.”
Let the baby pat and explore, and follow where they look.
activities.safety: Tape all edges securely and check daily so no pieces can be peeled off and mouthed.

activities.title: Crunchy Leaf Pile
materials: A small pile of large dry leaves, raked by educators
steps: Check the leaves first and remove sticks, litter, droppings, small stones and any mushrooms.
Sit beside the pile with a baby and scrunch a leaf: “Crunch!”
Wait to see if they reach, pat or kick the leaves.
Gently remove leaf bits from hands before they reach mouths.
activities.safety: Stay within arm's reach, watch closely for mouthing, and never let babies eat anything found outside.

activities.title: Sunny Window Shadows
materials: Large cardboard leaf shapes taped to the glass
steps: Notice where the shadows fall on the floor on a sunny morning.
Lay the baby or sit them nearby and wave your hand in the light.
Say “Shadow! Where did it go?” as you move your hand away.
Return at a different time to see the shadows move.
activities.safety: Keep babies out of direct strong sunlight through glass for long periods; cut-outs stay taped high on the glass.

activities.title: Under the Tree
materials: Large blanket in the shade of a tree
steps: Lie on the blanket on your back beside a baby.
Look up together and describe what moves: branches, leaves, birds.
Wait in silence sometimes; let the baby take it in.
Respond to their sounds and points as they share what they see.
activities.safety: Check the ground first; dress in layers for cool fall weather and keep babies under 6 months in shade.

activities.title: Fall Bottles
materials: Strong glue and tape for the lids
steps: Show the baby how the leaves swirl when you tip the bottle.
Roll it gently across the floor toward them.
Let them hold, roll or shake it, and name the colours.
Notice if they follow the leaves with their eyes.
activities.safety: Glue AND tape every lid; check daily and remove any bottle that cracks or leaks.

activities.title: Fall Walk Talk
steps: Walk slowly and stop often so babies can look.
Name what you see: a red tree, a squirrel, a puddle, falling leaves.
Point and wait for the baby to look or point too.
Wave hello to neighbours and talk about the weather.
activities.safety: Dress for the temperature; check straps and keep blankets away from faces.

activities.title: Our Fall Yard Book
materials: Photos of the babies outside, in a soft fabric photo book or board album
steps: Look through the photos with a baby on your lap.
Name the baby and what they were doing: “That's you in the leaves!”
Pause and let them pat the pictures.
Read a fall board book next, pointing to things you saw outside.

activities.title: Breezy Scarves
materials: Open outdoor space on a breezy day
steps: Hold a scarf up and let the wind catch it.
Say “Whoosh! The wind is blowing!”
Let crawlers chase a scarf you drag slowly; let sitters grab and wave.
Notice how babies respond to the feel of the breeze on their faces.
activities.safety: Scarves only with an educator present; collect them all after play. Dress for the weather.

activities.title: Big Pumpkin Pat
materials: One large whole pumpkin, washed, with the stem removed
steps: Set the pumpkin on the mat and pat it: “Big orange pumpkin!”
Invite babies to pat, push or lean on it.
Talk about how it feels: smooth, bumpy, cool, heavy.
Let a group gather around it and notice each other's patting.
activities.safety: Keep the pumpkin whole and uncut; this is touch-only, not food. Check every child's allergy list first, and wipe hands after.

schedule.focus: Out we go: fall walks, the shade of a tree and the colours of leaves
Wind, light and crunch: leaves to touch, breezes to chase, shadows to find

observe: What does each baby look at first when you go outside?
How does the baby react to the sound and feel of crunchy leaves?
Does the baby follow moving things with their eyes: leaves, shadows, birds?
How does the baby respond to wind or cool air on their face?
Who points, reaches or makes sounds to share something they noticed?
How does the baby's mood change outside compared with inside?
family: Ask families to send warm layers, a hat and a change of clothes for daily outdoor time.
Share a photo of their baby in the leaves, if the family has given consent.
Suggest a short fall walk at home, naming what they see together.
Invite families to bring a large leaf from their street for the leaf window.
Ask how families enjoy the outdoors in fall, and what words they use for leaves, trees and wind.
inclusion: Make sure outdoor spaces are reachable with strollers, adaptive seating and mobility equipment.
Bring nature inside for babies who can't go out on a given day: the leaf window and fall bottles.
For babies sensitive to cold or wind, offer shorter visits, extra layers and a sheltered spot.
For babies with low vision, choose bright, high-contrast leaves and describe sounds and textures in detail.
Offer sensory alternatives for babies who dislike certain textures, like watching leaves fall instead of touching the pile.
Talk with families and any resource consultant about outdoor comfort and any medical needs.

tips: Name leaf colours in both languages as you look: “Rouge, red!”
Label the leaf window with “Les feuilles d'automne.”
Invite families to share words for leaf, tree and wind in their home language.
Treat every point and sound as a baby's way of sharing, in any language.

safety_notes: Before every outdoor session, check the area for mushrooms, unknown berries, droppings, litter, sticks and small stones. Babies never eat anything found outside.
Dress babies in weather-appropriate layers and hats; keep babies under 6 months in the shade and out of direct sun.
Indoor nature items are large and sealed: leaves under taped contact paper or inside bottles with lids glued AND taped.
Watch closely for mouthing during all leaf play and remove small pieces from hands right away.

title: Board Books and Babble
summary: Language grows in warm, back-and-forth moments: a baby babbles, an adult answers, and the conversation goes on. This unit centres on board books, serve-and-return talk, puppets and simple signs and gestures, so every baby is heard and has more ways to communicate.
big_questions: How does each baby start a conversation with us?
What helps a baby stay interested in a book?
Which signs and gestures do babies use to tell us what they want?

goals.text: Babies take part in back-and-forth exchanges using sounds, looks and gestures.
Babies enjoy board books with a familiar adult and begin to handle books themselves.
Babies understand more words and respond to familiar names, routines and questions.
Babies use simple signs and gestures, like waving, pointing and “more”, to communicate.
Babies feel calm and close during cozy book and talk times.

activities.title: Serve and Return Chats
steps: Watch for the baby's “serve”: a look, a sound, a point.
Return it: name what they are looking at, or copy their sound.
Wait. Count to five in your head to give them a turn.
Keep the exchange going as long as the baby is interested.

activities.title: Lap Book Snuggle
materials: Sturdy board books with real photos or simple pictures
steps: Hold the baby on your lap so you can both see the pages.
Let the baby help turn pages, even if you skip ahead.
Point and name one thing per page; talk more than you read.
Stop when the baby wants to stop; a few pages is a success.

activities.title: Signs for More and All Done
materials: A favourite song or game babies ask for again
Picture card of each sign for educators
steps: Play a quick game the baby enjoys, like a bounce rhyme.
Stop and ask “More?” while making the sign.
Wait. Respond to any gesture, look or sound as a request.
When the game ends, sign and say “All done.”

activities.title: Lift-the-Flap Hunt
materials: Sturdy lift-the-flap board books with thick flaps
steps: Ask “Who's hiding?” and pause before you lift the flap.
Lift slowly and react with delight.
Guide the baby's hand to the next flap and wait for them to try.
Name what they find and make its sound.
activities.safety: Retire books with torn or loose flaps; paper pieces are a choking risk.

activities.title: Animal Sounds Book
materials: Board book with large animal photos
Large soft animal toys with sewn-on features
steps: Point to an animal and make its sound: “Moo!”
Pause and let the baby try the sound.
Match the toy to the picture and offer it to the baby.
Repeat favourite pages; babies love to know what comes next.
activities.safety: Soft toys must have embroidered eyes and no small parts.

activities.title: Book Basket Crawl
materials: Board books spread face-up across a firm mat
steps: Spread a few books across the floor, a little apart.
Invite crawlers and sitters to go to a book that catches their eye.
Join them where they land and talk about the cover.
Help them carry or push books back to the basket.

activities.title: Story Blanket Outside
materials: A small basket of board books
steps: Check the ground, then spread the blanket and settle with two or three babies.
Read a book and point to real things nearby that match: a tree, a bird.
Pause to listen to outdoor sounds and name them.
Let babies crawl, roll and return to the books as they like.
activities.safety: Shade for babies under 6 months; dress for the weather and watch for mouthing of anything found outside.

activities.title: Wave Hello, Wave Bye-Bye
steps: Wave and say hello to each baby as they arrive in play.
Wave together at the mirror, at a friend, at a toy you put away.
Wait for any wave back and celebrate it.
Use the same words and wave every time so babies learn the pattern.

activities.title: Puppet Talk
materials: Large hand puppet with sewn-on features
Low screen or cushion to hide behind
steps: Pop the puppet up and have it greet the baby by name.
Have the puppet ask a simple question, then wait.
Answer the baby's sounds through the puppet: “Oh, you said ba-ba!”
Let the baby touch and hold the puppet if they want.
activities.safety: Puppets must have embroidered features only and no loose threads.

activities.title: Words from Home
materials: A card for each baby with key words from home, written by their family
steps: Learn a few words each family uses, like milk, mama, bye-bye or a pet name.
Use those words with the baby during play and book time.
Watch how the baby responds to hearing a familiar home word.
Share with the family which words the baby seemed to know.

schedule.focus: Taking turns: serve-and-return talk, waving and first book snuggles
More ways to talk: signs, animal sounds, flaps and puppets

observe: How does each baby start a conversation: a look, a sound, a point, a reach?
How many turns does the baby take before looking away?
Which books does the baby choose again and again?
Is the baby using any signs or gestures on their own, like waving or reaching up?
Which home-language words does the baby respond to?
What new sounds or babbles have you heard this week?
family: Invite families to write down words and nicknames they use at home, in any language.
Lend a board book to take home for the weekend, if your centre has a lending basket.
Share the signs you're using (more, all done) so families can use them too.
Suggest narrating everyday moments at home: “Now we wash hands. Splash!”
Invite a family member to read or tell a short story in their home language.
inclusion: For babies who are hard of hearing, sign with every key word and face the baby when you talk.
For babies with low vision, choose high-contrast books, textured pages and lots of describing words.
Give extra waiting time for a response; some babies need longer to process and reply.
Offer books in a basket at floor level and in a book stand for babies who use supportive seating.
Honour every family's language: home language helps, not hinders, learning a second language.
Talk with families and any resource consultant if you have questions about a baby's communication.

tips: Keep a few French board books in the basket and read them as often as English ones.
Use the same sign with both languages: sign “more” while saying “more” and “encore”.
Invite families to record or write words in their home language and use them daily.
Accept and answer babbles in any language; every turn counts.

safety_notes: Use sturdy board or cloth books only; retire books with torn pages or loose flaps.
Puppets and soft toys must have sewn-on features and no small parts or ties longer than 15 cm.
Outdoors: check the ground first, use shade for babies under 6 months and dress for the weather.

title: All About My Family
summary: Toddlers learn who they are through the people who love them. This unit brings families into the room through photos, home routines, songs and home languages, so every child sees their own family reflected and valued. Families of every shape and size belong here.
big_questions: How do toddlers show us who matters to them?
What home routines and words help each child feel at home here?

goals.text: Children see their own family reflected in the room and point to, name or show interest in family members.
Children feel calm and secure when familiar home words, songs and routines are part of the day.
Children act out simple home routines in pretend play, alone or beside a friend.
Children hear and respond to greetings and words from many home languages.
Children move their bodies with confidence while exploring indoors and out.

activities.title: Family Photo Wall
materials: Laminating sleeves or clear contact paper
Low wall space at child height
steps: Mount each child's covered family photo flat on the wall at toddler eye level.
Sit near the wall and wait for children to come and look.
Name the people a child points to, using the words their family uses.
Notice who returns to the wall during the day, especially at drop-off.
activities.safety: Cover photos fully and tape every edge flat so there are no loose corners to peel and mouth.

activities.title: Our Family Board Book
materials: Homemade book with one laminated page per child's family
Sturdy rings or a bound binder
Board books showing many kinds of families
steps: Invite one or two children to cuddle up and look at the book.
Turn to a child's page and say, "Here is your family."
Pause and wait for pointing, words or signs.
Read a board book showing other family shapes and talk about what you see.
activities.safety: Keep binder rings closed and checked; store the book where it can be reached but not chewed apart.

activities.title: Baby Doll Bath Time
materials: Washable baby dolls with a range of skin tones
Low tub with a little warm water
steps: Set the tub on a towel on the floor with dolls nearby.
Model gently washing a doll's hands and feet while you talk.
Follow children's lead as they wash, dry and wrap dolls.
Ask, "Who gives you a bath at home?" and listen.
activities.safety: Water play only with an educator within arm's reach; use shallow water and tip it out when done.

activities.title: Neighbourhood Wave Walk
steps: Take a short walk past homes, shops or the park near the centre.
Wave and say hello to neighbours you pass.
Point out doors, windows and pets: "Who lives here?"
Back inside, talk about the homes you saw.
activities.safety: Count children before, during and after the walk; use sun protection or warm layers as the weather needs.

activities.title: Hello in Many Languages
materials: List of greetings families have shared, written how they sound
Hand drum or large sealed shaker
steps: Gather children and tap a gentle beat on the drum.
Sing a simple hello song using one family's greeting.
Show that family's photo as you sing their word.
Repeat with a new greeting each day.
activities.safety: Any shaker must be large and sealed, with the lid glued and taped.

activities.title: Big Box House
materials: Large cardboard box with a cut-out door and windows
Wide tape to cover cut edges
steps: Place the box house in an open space.
Invite children to crawl in, peek out and knock on the door.
Offer crayons to draw on the walls of the house.
Play peek-a-boo through the windows.
activities.safety: Tape all cut edges and remove staples; limit the house to two or three children at a time.

activities.title: Home Kitchen Pretend
materials: Empty, clean food boxes and tins families send from home
steps: Add the boxes and tins families brought, including labels in home languages.
Join the play and cook beside the children.
Name the foods: "This is from Mia's house."
Notice who stirs, pours, feeds dolls or shares.
activities.safety: Check tins have smooth rims with no sharp edges and boxes are clean and empty.

activities.title: Take the Babies for a Walk
steps: Bring toy strollers and dolls to the yard.
Invite children to push their "family" along the path.
Call out simple directions: "Go slow", "Stop", "Turn around."
Rest together and talk about where the babies went.
activities.safety: Use sun protection or warm clothing; keep pushing areas clear of trip hazards.

activities.title: Lullabies From Home
materials: Songs or lullabies families have shared (sung or recorded by a family member)
steps: Dim the lights a little and spread out the blanket.
Sing or play one family's lullaby.
Say whose family shared it.
Rock, sway or pat gently and let children rest close.

schedule.focus: Who is in my family? Faces, names and hellos.
What we do at home: routines, cooking, songs and languages.

observe: Which family members does each child point to or name on the photo wall?
How does a child react when they hear their home language greeting?
What home routines show up in pretend play (bathing, cooking, rocking)?
Who looks at the photo wall during drop-off or when missing home?
Does a child play beside a friend, copy them, or share a pot or doll?
What words, signs or gestures does a child use for family members?
family: Invite each family to share one or two photos of the people (and pets) at home; offer to take a photo at pick-up if printing is hard.
Ask families for a greeting, a lullaby or a favourite song in their home language.
Request clean, empty food boxes or tins from home for the play kitchen.
Share a photo of their child at the photo wall with a short note about what they said or did.
Ask what each family calls grandparents, parents and siblings so educators use the same words.
inclusion: Hang photos and books at sitting height and at a wheelchair-friendly level so every child can reach them.
Pair spoken family words with simple signs or gestures (mom, dad, baby, love).
Offer a personal family photo in a soft pocket a child can carry for comfort during transitions.
Give extra time to respond after you ask a question; accept pointing, signs and home-language words.
Talk with the family and any resource consultant about routines or words that help their child feel settled.

tips: Label the photo wall with "Ma famille" and add the child's name.
Sing the hello song in English, French and each child's home language.
Ask families how they say mom, dad and grandparent at home and use those words too.
Accept answers in any language; repeat back what the child said with a smile.

safety_notes: Families decide which photos are shared; keep them in the room and out of social media without written consent.
Use the words each family uses for its members; never assume who is in a family.
Check donated boxes and tins for sharp edges and remove any small parts before play.

title: Colours Everywhere
summary: Toddlers notice colour long before they can name it. This unit invites them to find, match, mix and move with colour through paint, water, fabric and the world outside. Short, repeated, hands-on experiences build colour words and a love of making a mess with purpose.
big_questions: Which colours catch each child's eye, and how do they show us?
What happens when toddlers mix two colours together?

goals.text: Children notice, point to and begin to name a few colours in their world.
Children match and sort large objects by colour.
Children explore paint and colour mixing with their hands and big brushes, and see what changes.
Children share a favourite colour and enjoy colour games with friends.
Children move with energy and joy using colourful scarves and outdoor play.

activities.title: Red Things Basket
materials: Large red objects (block, soft ball, cup, fabric square)
steps: Show the basket of red things and say "red" as you lift each one.
Hide a few red items around the room at child height.
Invite children to find and bring them back.
Choose a new colour on another day.
activities.safety: Use only items bigger than a choke-tube tester; check the room for small items before play.

activities.title: Two-Colour Finger Painting
materials: Non-toxic washable paint in red and yellow (later blue and yellow)
Large paper taped to the table
steps: Put a blob of each colour on the paper.
Invite children to touch, spread and swirl.
Notice aloud when a new colour appears: "Look, orange!"
Hang paintings low so children can see them.
activities.safety: Washable, non-toxic paint only; stay close and redirect hands away from mouths.

activities.title: Taste-Safe Yogurt Paint
materials: Plain yogurt (or a dairy-free yogurt that suits every child's list)
steps: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first, and choose a yogurt that is safe for the whole group.
Mix a few colours in bowls with the children watching.
Invite children to paint on trays with fingers or big brushes.
Wash hands well before and after.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first; if any child cannot have the yogurt, use washable paint for the group instead.

activities.title: Colour Sorting Bins
materials: Three bins lined with matching coloured paper
steps: Start with two colours only.
Model putting a block in the bin of the same colour and name it.
Invite children to fill and dump; sorting may come later.
Add the third colour when children are ready.

activities.title: Colour Bottles in the Window
materials: Strong glue and tape for the lids
steps: Make the bottles ahead: fill, colour, glue the lid and tape it.
Set them where light shines through.
Invite children to roll, shake and look through them.
Hold two bottles together and wonder what colour you see.
activities.safety: Lids glued AND taped; check bottles daily for cracks or leaks and remove any damaged ones.

activities.title: Scarf Colour Dance
materials: Lightweight play scarves in several colours
steps: Let each child choose a scarf and name its colour together.
Wave, toss and catch scarves to the music.
Call a colour: "Blue scarves up high!"
Finish by floating scarves down slowly.
activities.safety: Scarves are never tied around necks or bodies; collect them when the dance ends.

activities.title: Colour Walk and Chalk
materials: Sun hats and sunscreen or warm layers
Clipboard to note what children find
steps: Walk the yard and point out colours: green grass, blue sky, red door.
Pause for each child's finds.
Offer chunky chalk to colour the path together.
Name the colours on the big group drawing.
activities.safety: Sun protection or weather-appropriate clothing; no picking or tasting plants, and never eat anything found outside.

activities.title: Colour Peek-a-Boo Book
materials: Homemade board book with large felt flaps sewn or glued on
Photos of familiar things in bold colours
steps: Read with one or two children on your lap or beside you.
Ask, "What is under the blue flap?"
Wait, then lift together and name the colour and object.
Let children turn pages and lift flaps themselves.
activities.safety: Check flaps are firmly attached and there are no loose pieces.

activities.title: Rainbow Water Tubs
steps: Tint each tub a different colour.
Invite children to pour and scoop.
Pour a little blue into yellow and watch together.
Tip out water when done and dry the floor.
activities.safety: Water play only with an educator within arm's reach; tip out water when done and wipe up spills.

activities.title: My Favourite Colour Wall
steps: Offer each child a choice of two or three coloured squares.
Take a photo of the child holding their favourite.
Mount the photos together on a low wall.
Visit the wall and say, "Sam likes green."

schedule.focus: Finding and naming colours around us.
Mixing colours and making new ones.

observe: Which colours does each child reach for first, again and again?
Does a child point to, sign or say a colour word? Which ones?
How does a child react when two paints blend into a new colour?
Who sorts by colour, and who prefers filling and dumping?
How does a child use their whole body during the scarf dance?
Who looks to a friend or copies a friend while painting or sorting?
family: Invite families to send a photo of something in their child's favourite colour at home.
Share a short note on colour words to use at bath time or getting dressed ("your blue socks").
Ask families how they say colours in their home language and add the words to the room.
Suggest a free colour walk at home or on the way to the centre.
Send home a painting with a note about what the child noticed or said.
inclusion: Offer big brushes, chunky chalk and foam grips for children who need a larger grip.
For children who avoid messy hands, offer a brush, a roller or paint on a tray with a spoon.
Use high-contrast colours and name the object too, not only the colour, for children who see colour differently.
Show a simple picture sequence (smock on, paint, wash hands) for messy play.
Talk with the family and any resource consultant about sensory preferences.

tips: Label the sorting bins in English and French ("rouge / red").
Play the scarf dance calling colours in French on some days.
Invite families to share colour words in their home language for the favourite colour wall.
Accept any language or a point as a correct answer.

safety_notes: Use only non-toxic, washable art materials; no small craft items for this age group.
Food-based paint: check every child's allergy and dietary list first; no peanuts or tree nuts, and wash hands before and after.
Sensory bottles must have lids glued and taped; inspect them daily.
Water play only with an educator within arm's reach; tip out water when done.

title: Down on the Farm
summary: Farm animals are a toddler favourite: big sounds, big movements and lots of pretend play. This unit uses songs, puppets, sensory play and movement to build animal words and sounds, and links farms to the foods and families children know. Spring is a natural time to talk about baby animals and growing things.
big_questions: Which animals and sounds spark each child's interest?
How do toddlers use pretend play to take care of animals?

goals.text: Children imitate animal sounds and begin to name some farm animals.
Children use toy animals and props in simple pretend play, beside or with friends.
Children move like animals and build strength, balance and coordination.
Children explore textures, mud and water with curiosity.
Children connect farms to the foods and places their families know.

activities.title: Barnyard Song With Puppets
materials: Farm animal hand puppets with stitched eyes
Basket or barn box to hide puppets
steps: Pull one puppet from the barn box.
Sing a simple farm song and pause before each sound.
Wait for children to moo, oink or baa.
Let children choose the next animal.
activities.safety: Use puppets with stitched, not glued-on, eyes and features.

activities.title: Who Says That?
steps: Lay out two or three animal cards.
Make one animal sound.
Invite children to point to the animal that makes it.
Swap roles: a child makes the sound, you find the card.

activities.title: Big Barn Play
materials: Large farm animal figures bigger than a choke-tube tester
steps: Set up the barn on a low table or the floor.
Watch how children move the animals.
Join in with a story: "The cow is sleepy. Where does she go?"
Add fences with blocks if children are interested.
activities.safety: Check every figure against a choke-tube tester; remove any small or broken pieces.

activities.title: Muddy Pig Wash
steps: Let children roll pigs in the brown "mud" on a tray.
Move to the tub and wash the pigs clean.
Talk about dirty and clean, wet and dry.
Tip out the water when done.
activities.safety: Water play only with an educator within arm's reach; use non-toxic washable paint; tip out water when done.

activities.title: Crawl Into the Barn
materials: Large cardboard box decorated as a barn
steps: Set up the tunnel leading into the barn box.
Invite children to crawl through like piglets or puppies.
Cheer them out the other side.
Change the animal each round.
activities.safety: Use soft mats and let one child through the tunnel at a time.

activities.title: Move Like a Farm Animal
steps: Show one card and model the movement: gallop, waddle, hop.
Move together across the yard.
Stop and rest like a sleepy cow.
Let a child pick the next card.
activities.safety: Sun protection and weather-appropriate clothing; check the yard for hazards first.

activities.title: Egg Collecting Basket
materials: Large wooden or fabric eggs bigger than a choke-tube tester
steps: Hide eggs in easy places before children arrive.
Tell children the hen has laid eggs.
Collect eggs in baskets.
Count them together: "One, two, three!"
activities.safety: Eggs must be larger than a choke-tube tester; count them in and out.

activities.title: Farm Foods Tasting
materials: Plain yogurt only if safe for every child
Pictures of where each food comes from
steps: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first.
Wash hands together.
Show each picture, then offer the matching food at the table.
Talk about tastes and textures; children choose what to try.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first; no peanuts or tree nuts; cut food small and soft; children seated and supervised while eating.

activities.title: Who's in the Barn? Flap Book
materials: Homemade board book with felt flaps on barn doors
steps: Read with a small group on the carpet.
Knock on each barn door and ask, "Who's inside?"
Lift the flap and make the animal's sound together.
Leave the book out for children to explore.
activities.safety: Check flaps are firmly attached.

activities.title: Feed the Hungry Animals
materials: Cardboard boxes painted as animal faces with big cut-out mouths
Large soft balls or fabric "hay" bundles
steps: Stand the animal boxes against a wall.
Invite children to post the "food" into the mouths.
Make munching sounds when food goes in.
Open the box and count the food together.
activities.safety: Tape cut edges smooth; use only large soft items for "food".

activities.title: Woolly Sheep Touch Board
materials: Board with large fabric pieces glued and stapled down (fleece, corduroy, faux fur)
Animal pictures next to each texture
steps: Sit with children by the board.
Touch each fabric and say: soft, bumpy, fluffy.
Link the texture to an animal: "Soft like a sheep."
Invite children to find their favourite.
activities.safety: Check fabric pieces daily; remove any that are lifting so they cannot be pulled off and mouthed.

activities.title: Tractors in the Sandbox
steps: Rake the sandbox and check it before play.
Offer tractors and shovels.
Talk about digging, pushing and filling.
Wash hands when you come in.
activities.safety: Keep the sandbox covered when not in use; check for animal waste and litter before play; wash hands afterward.

activities.title: Farms and Markets Photo Story
materials: Photos families share of farms, gardens, markets or animals they know
Large map or simple poster board
steps: Show one family's photo at circle.
Say whose family shared it and what it shows.
Invite children to point and name animals or foods.
Add the photo to the poster.

activities.title: Paint the Big Red Barn
steps: Lay the barn flat on a floor covering.
Paint it red together, side by side.
Talk about big strokes and little dabs.
Stand it up and add it to the farm play area.
activities.safety: Washable, non-toxic paint; stay close to redirect mouthing.

schedule.focus: Meeting the animals: names and sounds.
Caring for animals: feeding, washing and the barn.
Food from farms and the farms our families know.

observe: Which animal sounds does each child make, and when do they start making them before you do?
How does a child use the barn and animals: lining up, feeding, putting to sleep?
Who plays alongside a friend at the barn, and do they copy or hand each other animals?
How does a child respond to the textures and the muddy paint: eager, cautious, curious?
Which animal movements can a child try (gallop, hop, waddle)?
Does a child point to or name foods during the tasting?
family: Invite families to share photos or stories of farms, gardens or markets they know, here or in another country.
Ask families what animal sounds are in their home language (a rooster sounds different in many languages!).
Suggest a free trip to a local farmers' market or park with ducks, if it suits them.
Send home the words of the barnyard song.
Ask families about foods their child enjoys, and about allergies, before the tasting week.
inclusion: Offer animal cards with real photos and simple signs for each animal.
For children who avoid messy play, offer the pig wash with a brush or sponge on a long handle.
Make tunnel play optional; let a child watch or roll a ball through first.
Give extra wait time after you make a sound; any sound, sign or point counts.
Make sure the barn play area is reachable from a seat or standing frame.
Talk with the family and any resource consultant about sensory and movement needs.

tips: Sing the barnyard song in French too, using the French animal names.
Compare animal sounds: a rooster says "cocorico" in French. Invite families to share sounds from their home language.
Label the barn area: "la ferme / the farm".
Accept any language, sound or point as an answer.

safety_notes: Farm figures, eggs and props must all be bigger than a choke-tube tester; check them before each use.
Food tasting: check every child's allergy and dietary list first; no peanuts or tree nuts; cut food small and soft for toddlers.
Water play only with an educator within arm's reach; tip out water when done.
If visiting a real farm or petting animals, wash hands with soap and water right after and keep hands away from mouths.

title: Snow and Mittens
summary: Snow is a whole new world for toddlers: cold, crunchy, melting and full of tracks. This unit offers short, well-supervised snow and ice play, lots of dressing practice, and warm, cozy moments to come back to. Children build independence, words for cold and warm, and comfort being outside in winter.
big_questions: What do toddlers notice when they touch, step on and watch snow and ice?
How can we help each child feel confident getting dressed for the cold?

goals.text: Children explore snow and ice with their senses for short, supervised times.
Children try parts of dressing for outdoors, like pulling on mittens or a hat.
Children use words, signs or gestures for cold, warm, snow and clothing.
Children help each other and the group during winter routines.
Children move with confidence in the snow, stomping, walking and pushing.

activities.title: Snow Tracks Walk
materials: Warm outdoor clothing for each child
steps: Walk slowly across fresh snow together.
Stomp, then turn and look at your footprints.
Compare big educator tracks and small child tracks.
Look for bird or animal tracks too.
activities.safety: Check the weather and wind chill first; keep the time short in very cold weather; never eat snow; watch for cold, wet hands.

activities.title: Snow in the Bin
materials: Low bin of clean snow brought inside
steps: Offer mittens and invite children to scoop and pat the snow.
Talk about cold, soft and wet.
Check back after ten minutes: what happened to the snow?
Warm hands with a towel and a cuddle.
activities.safety: Keep it brief (5–10 minutes) with an educator within arm's reach; never eat snow; warm and dry hands after; tip out melt water when done.

activities.title: Frozen Toy Rescue
materials: Large ice block frozen in a loaf pan with big toys inside
Squeeze bottles of warm (not hot) water
steps: Set the ice block on a tray.
Wonder aloud: "How can we get the toys out?"
Squeeze warm water onto the ice and watch it melt.
Celebrate each rescued toy, then tip out the water.
activities.safety: Toys inside must be bigger than a choke-tube tester; water play with an educator within arm's reach; test water temperature; tip out water when done.

activities.title: Mitten Match-Up
materials: Five or six pairs of clean mittens in different colours
steps: Mix the mittens in the basket.
Pull one out and ask, "Where's the friend?"
Help children find the matching mitten.
Lay pairs side by side and name the colours.
activities.safety: Use mittens with no cords or clips longer than 15 cm.

activities.title: Coat Flip Practice
steps: Lay the coat on the floor, open, with the hood by the child's feet.
Child puts arms in the sleeves.
Flip the coat up over the head and on.
Cheer the effort, not just success.

activities.title: Painting Big Ice Blocks
materials: Large ice blocks frozen in loaf pans or tubs
Non-toxic washable liquid watercolour or paint
steps: Set a big ice block on a tray.
Invite children to paint and watch colours run.
Talk about slippery, cold and drippy.
Tip out the melt water when done.
activities.safety: Use only big ice blocks, never cubes, for toddlers; educator within arm's reach; tip out water when done.

activities.title: Indoor Snowball Toss
materials: Soft white fabric balls or large rolled-up socks
steps: Scatter the "snowballs" on the floor.
Toss them into the basket.
Step back a little for children who want a challenge.
Count snowballs back into the basket.
activities.safety: Use only soft, large balls; play in a clear space.

activities.title: Dress the Bear
materials: Felt board with a large bear shape
Large felt winter clothes (coat, hat, mittens, boots) bigger than a choke-tube tester
Board book about dressing for snow
steps: Read the book together.
Say, "Bear is going outside. What does Bear need?"
Invite children to add clothes to the bear.
Name each piece in English and French.
activities.safety: All felt pieces must be larger than a choke-tube tester.

activities.title: Warm-Up Cuddle Corner
steps: After outdoor play, gather in the cozy corner.
Sing a warm-up song naming body parts: "Warm my hands, warm my toes."
Rub hands together and wiggle toes.
Read a short winter book.

activities.title: Little Snow Shovellers
materials: Warm outdoor clothing and neck warmers
steps: Show children a small path to clear.
Shovel together, side by side.
Fill buckets and dump them in a pile.
Thank helpers by name.
activities.safety: Check weather and wind chill; keep sessions short; space children apart while shovelling; never eat snow.

schedule.focus: First touches: snow, tracks and getting dressed.
Ice and melting, and helping each other outside.

observe: How does a child react to touching snow: eager, cautious, or wanting to watch first?
Which steps of dressing can a child try on their own (mittens, hat, coat flip)?
What words, signs or gestures does a child use for cold, warm and wet?
Does a child notice melting or tracks and show you?
Who helps a friend, or hands a friend a mitten?
How long does a child stay comfortable outside, and what are their signs of being cold?
family: Share a list of winter clothing to keep at the centre (two pairs of mittens, neck warmer, snow pants, boots) and point families to local clothing exchanges.
Send home the coat flip trick with a photo so children can practise at home.
Ask families to label mittens and boots.
Invite families to share winter words or traditions from their home or home country.
Share a photo of their child playing in the snow with a note about what they noticed.
inclusion: Use a picture sequence for dressing (snow pants, boots, coat, hat, mittens) and take it outside.
Offer extra time and a calm space for dressing; break it into one step at a time.
For children who dislike cold or wet hands, offer scoops, a brush or watching from beside the bin.
Make sure paths are cleared for walkers, wagons and mobility devices; offer snow in a bin at seated height.
Talk with the family and any resource consultant about sensory needs and clothing that works best.

tips: Name clothes in French as children dress: "ta tuque, tes mitaines".
Label cubbies and the dressing picture sequence in both languages.
Sing the warm-up song in French on some days.
Invite families to share winter clothing words in their home language; accept answers in any language.

safety_notes: Check temperature and wind chill before going out and follow your centre's cold-weather policy; keep outdoor time short in extreme cold.
Use neck warmers, not scarves, and no mitten cords or clips longer than 15 cm.
Never eat snow or ice; snow and ice play is brief, supervised, and followed by warm, dry hands.
Use large ice blocks only (no ice cubes) and toys bigger than a choke-tube tester; tip out melt water when done.

title: Bugs in the Garden
summary: Toddlers are fascinated by small moving creatures. This unit invites them to look closely at worms, ants and ladybugs outside, practise gentle hands, and explore bugs through movement, art and song. It builds early care for living things and a sense of wonder about the garden.
big_questions: What do toddlers notice when they watch a bug up close?
How do toddlers learn to be gentle with living things?

goals.text: Children watch insects and worms with curiosity and point out what they notice.
Children practise gentle hands with living things and with each other.
Children move their bodies like bugs: wiggling, crawling and buzzing.
Children explore paint, soil and water as they make bug art and help in the garden.
Children feel part of a group that cares for the garden.

activities.title: Bug Hunt With Viewers
materials: Clear bug viewer containers with lids
steps: Walk the garden edge and look low: under leaves, along the path.
Educator gently lifts a log or stone while children watch.
Educator places a bug in a viewer for a short look.
Return every bug where you found it.
activities.safety: Educators handle the bugs; avoid bees, wasps and stinging insects; no touching plants or mushrooms you don't know; never eat anything found outside; wash hands after.

activities.title: Worm Watch
materials: Damp soil in a shallow tray
A few worms found after rain
steps: Place the worms on the damp soil tray outside.
Watch them stretch and wiggle together.
Children may touch gently with one finger if they choose.
Return the worms to the garden and wash hands.
activities.safety: Keep the worms' visit short and damp; educator holds the spray bottle and stays within arm's reach; one-finger gentle touch only; wash hands with soap and water right after.

activities.title: Wiggle Like a Worm
steps: Lie on the mats and wiggle like worms.
Curl up small, then stretch out long.
Wiggle forward slowly to the music.
Rest still, like a sleepy worm.

activities.title: Ladybug Dot Painting
steps: Show a ladybug picture and count the spots together.
Invite children to dot black spots on the red circles.
Name "dot, dot, dot" as they go.
Hang the ladybugs low on the wall.
activities.safety: Washable, non-toxic paint; check markers have caps too large to swallow.

activities.title: Big Bug Sort
materials: Large toy insects bigger than a choke-tube tester
A green leaf mat and a flower mat
steps: Spread the toy bugs on the floor.
Name each bug as children pick it up.
Invite children to put bugs on the leaf or the flower.
Sort by colour if interest grows.
activities.safety: Check every toy bug against a choke-tube tester; remove any with loose legs or wings.

activities.title: Butterfly Fold Prints
materials: Large paper butterfly shapes, folded in half
Two or three colours of washable paint
steps: Open the butterfly flat.
Invite children to spoon paint onto one side.
Fold and press with both hands.
Open together and say, "Wow, both wings match!"
activities.safety: Washable, non-toxic paint only.

activities.title: Planting the Bug Garden
materials: Large planter tub or garden bed
Child-safe seedlings (such as sunflowers or marigolds) already sprouted
steps: Dig holes together in the soil.
Educator places each seedling; children pat the soil around it.
Water with watering cans.
Visit the garden each day to look for bugs.
activities.safety: Use seedlings, not loose seeds; choose plants known to be safe for children; educator within arm's reach of water; tip out water when done; wash hands after soil play.

activities.title: Little Bug Fingerplay
materials: Soft bug puppet with stitched features
steps: Sing a short bug rhyme with finger movements (crawl, fly, hide).
Use the puppet to crawl up an arm.
Pause before the last word and let children fill it in.
Repeat it often across the week.

activities.title: Gentle Hands Practice
steps: Show soft, gentle petting on the toy bug.
Pass it around the circle: "Gentle hands."
Practise gentle touches on a friend's arm, only if the friend says yes.
Notice and name gentle moments during the day.

activities.title: Buzzing Bee Flower Hop
materials: Large paper flowers taped flat on the floor
steps: Invite children to buzz like bees between the flowers.
When the music stops, land on a flower.
Name the flower's colour.
Move the flowers farther apart for a bigger challenge.
activities.safety: Tape flowers flat so no one slips.

schedule.focus: Looking closely: who lives in the garden?
Caring for bugs and our own bug garden.

observe: What does a child notice about a bug: legs, colour, how it moves?
How does a child approach a worm: close and curious, or watching from a distance?
When does a child use gentle hands without a reminder?
What words, signs or sounds does a child use for bugs?
Who shows a friend a bug or calls you over to see?
How does a child use their body to move like a bug?
family: Invite families to take a short bug walk on the way home and share what they spot.
Ask families for bug words in their home language.
Share photos of their child watching worms or planting.
Send home the bug fingerplay so families can do it together.
Invite a family member who gardens to visit and help plant.
inclusion: Bring bugs in viewers to a child at seated or lying height.
Offer a long-handled trowel or a larger grip for planting.
For children who are worried about bugs, offer toy bugs and pictures first and let them watch from a distance.
Use photos and signs for bug, gentle, look and wash hands.
Talk with the family and any resource consultant about sensory needs around soil, paint and wet hands.

tips: Label the bug viewers and garden in both languages ("le jardin / the garden").
Sing the bug fingerplay in French too.
Invite families to share bug words in their home language.
Accept any language, sign or point as an answer.

safety_notes: Educators handle insects; children watch in viewers and touch only worms, gently, if they choose. Avoid stinging insects.
Never eat anything found outside; no picking unknown berries, mushrooms or plants; use only plants known to be safe for children.
Sun protection and weather-appropriate clothing every day outside; wash hands after soil and bug play.
Toy bugs must be bigger than a choke-tube tester; water play with an educator within arm's reach.

title: Feelings and Friends
summary: Toddlers feel big feelings before they have words for them. This unit helps children notice and name a few feelings, try simple calming tools, and practise turn-taking with lots of adult support. Friendship at this age starts with playing side by side, and that is something to celebrate.
big_questions: How do toddlers show us what they feel?
What helps each child feel calm again after a big feeling?

goals.text: Children notice and name a few feelings in themselves and others.
Children try simple calming tools with an educator's help.
Children take short turns and wait with support.
Children play beside and with friends and show interest in others.
Children use their bodies, art and music to express how they feel.

activities.title: Feelings Mirror
materials: Feelings photo cards with real faces
steps: Sit with a child or two in front of the mirror.
Make a happy face and say, "I feel happy."
