Invite children to copy, then try sad and surprised.
Name what you see: "Your eyes are big!"

activities.title: Our Faces Feelings Book
materials: Photos of the children showing different feelings (with family consent)
Laminated pages in a sturdy binder
steps: Read with one or two children at a time.
Point to a face: "Leo looks sad. What happened?"
Wait and listen to any words, signs or sounds.
Leave the book in the cozy corner.
activities.safety: Keep binder rings closed and checked.

activities.title: Calm-Down Bottles
materials: Water, clear dish soap and a drop of food colouring
Strong glue and tape for the lids
steps: Make the bottles ahead and seal them.
Show children how to shake and watch the bubbles settle.
Breathe slowly together while the bottle settles.
Keep the bottles in the cozy corner.
activities.safety: Lids glued AND taped; check daily for cracks or leaks and remove any damaged bottle.

activities.title: Smell the Flower, Blow the Candle
materials: Large picture card of a flower
Large picture card of a candle
steps: Hold up the flower: breathe in slowly through the nose.
Hold up the candle: blow out slowly.
Do it three times together.
Use it during the day when a child feels upset.

activities.title: Roll the Ball, Say a Name
materials: Carpet squares or a circle mat to sit on
steps: Sit in a small circle with legs out.
Say a child's name and roll the ball to them.
Help them roll it to a friend and say the friend's name.
Keep the circle small and the game short.

activities.title: My Turn, Your Turn
materials: Two of a favourite toy (two trucks, two dolls)
Picture card showing "my turn / your turn"
steps: Play with one child and model: "My turn... your turn."
Keep turns very short at first.
Use the picture card as a reminder.
Notice and name waiting: "You waited. Now it's your turn!"

activities.title: If You're Happy Song
steps: Sing the familiar happy song with claps.
Add new verses: sad (rub eyes), mad (stomp feet), sleepy (yawn).
Show the matching feelings card for each verse.
Let children choose the next feeling.

activities.title: Building the Cozy Corner
materials: Feelings photo cards at child height
steps: Set up a quiet corner with the children watching or helping.
Invite them to try the cushions and books.
Explain: "This is a place to feel calm."
Offer the corner as a choice, never as a punishment.

activities.title: Puppet Problem Solvers
materials: Two hand puppets with stitched features
steps: Act out both puppets wanting the same truck.
Have one puppet look sad and say so.
Ask, "What can they do?" and wait.
Try the children's ideas: take turns, find another truck, play together.

activities.title: Stomp and Freeze Outside
steps: Stomp like you feel mad while the drum plays loud.
Freeze when the drum stops.
Tiptoe softly when the drum plays quietly.
End with big slow breaths.
activities.safety: Sun protection or weather-appropriate clothing; check the space is clear of hazards.

activities.title: Friendship Parachute
materials: Small play parachute or large bedsheet
steps: Everyone holds the edge with an educator beside each small group.
Lift up high and bring it down slow.
Bounce the soft ball on top together.
Peek at friends under the parachute.
activities.safety: Keep the parachute low; never let children go underneath while others are pulling it down; sun protection outside.

activities.title: Helping Hands Tidy-Up
steps: Sing the tidy-up song.
Work beside children, putting toys in bins.
Thank helpers by name: "Ana helped Kai!"
Notice and name kindness out loud.

activities.title: Painting Fast and Slow Music
materials: Large paper taped to the table
steps: Play fast, bouncy music and paint quick lines.
Switch to slow, calm music and paint slow swirls.
Talk about how each song feels.
Hang paintings with the feeling words.
activities.safety: Washable, non-toxic paint; stay close to redirect mouthing.

activities.title: Choose-Your-Hello Board
materials: Picture board by the door: wave, high five, hug, smile
steps: At arrival, point to the board and ask how the child wants to say hello.
Respect the choice, including no touch.
Model asking friends too: "High five or wave?"
Use the board each morning.

schedule.focus: Naming feelings: happy, sad, mad.
Calming tools and the cozy corner.
Friends: turns, helping and solving problems together.

observe: How does a child show a big feeling: words, sounds, body movements?
Who does a child look to or move toward when upset?
Which calming tool does a child choose, and does it help?
How long can a child wait for a turn with support?
Who plays beside a friend, copies them, or offers a toy?
Does a child notice when a friend is sad, and what do they do?
Which feeling words, signs or faces does a child use or point to?
family: Share the "smell the flower, blow the candle" breathing so families can use it at home.
Ask families how their child shows feelings and what comforts them.
Invite families to share feeling words in their home language.
Ask for consent before using children's photos in the feelings book.
Share a photo of their child playing with a friend, and what you noticed.
inclusion: Use real-photo feelings cards and simple signs (happy, sad, mad, help, stop).
Offer a quieter space and noise-reducing options for children who are overwhelmed by sound.
Use first/then language: "First Ana's turn, then your turn."
Give extra processing time and accept any way of communicating a feeling.
Offer hand-over-hand help only with the child's consent and the family's agreement.
Talk with the family and any resource consultant about what helps their child regulate.

tips: Label the feelings cards in English and French.
Sing the happy song in French too ("Si tu es content...").
Invite families to share feeling words in their home language and add them to the cozy corner.
Accept any language, sign or face as an answer.

safety_notes: Calm-down bottles must have lids glued AND taped; inspect them daily.
The cozy corner is always a choice, never a time-out or punishment.
Get family consent before photographing children for the feelings book or displays.
Parachute play: keep it low and supervised, with an educator beside each small group.

title: Apples and Harvest Time
summary: Fall in Ontario is harvest time. Children explore apples and pumpkins with all their senses, count, sort, cook and pretend, then think about the people who grow our food and the things they feel thankful for. It connects everyday food to farms, families and the changing season.
big_questions: Where does our food come from before it reaches our table?
What changes do we notice in apples and pumpkins when we look inside, cook or leave them?
What are we thankful for this fall?

goals.text: Children use their senses to describe apples and pumpkins with new words (crunchy, smooth, sour, heavy).
Children count, compare and sort harvest items by colour, size and weight.
Children practise hand washing and safe food habits as part of cooking and tasting together.
Children share family harvest foods and traditions, and see their own families reflected in the room.
Children name people and things they are thankful for and show care for others.

activities.title: Apple Taste Test
materials: Three kinds of apples (red, green, yellow)
Cutting board and knife (adult use only)
Simple picture chart with three columns
steps: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first, and wash hands together.
Show the whole apples. Invite children to describe colour, size and smell.
An adult slices the apples into thin pieces away from the children. Offer a taste of each.
Ask: crunchy or soft? sweet or sour? Let each child place a sticker under their favourite.
Count the stickers together and talk about which apple most friends liked.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first; no nuts; adults cut apples into thin slices; seat children while eating; offer a different fruit or a non-food role to any child who cannot have apples.

activities.title: Apple Print Painting
materials: Apples cut in half by an adult (some across, some top to bottom)
Washable non-toxic paint in shallow trays
steps: Show both apple halves. Ask children what shape they see inside the cross-cut one.
Invite children to dip an apple half in paint and press it on paper.
Notice the star shape and the seeds. Name the parts: skin, flesh, core, seeds.
Let children mix prints with brushes or fingers however they like.
activities.safety: Painting apples are for art only and go in the compost after; adults do all cutting; remind children not to eat the painted apples.

activities.title: How Many Seeds?
materials: Several apples cut in half by an adult
steps: Give each small group an apple half on a tray. Invite children to guess how many seeds are inside.
Look closely with a magnifier. Count the seeds together, touching each one with a finger.
Match the count to a number card. Compare: which apple had the most?
Write each guess and each count on a chart so children can see them side by side.
activities.safety: Apple seeds are small: seeds stay on the tray, for children who no longer mouth objects, with supervision. Seeds are not for eating. Gather and discard all seeds at the end.

activities.title: Harvest Market
materials: A few real small pumpkins and squash
Toy cash register or a box with paper money
steps: Set up a market stand in dramatic play. Ask children what a market needs.
Invite children to take roles: farmer, shopper, cashier, delivery driver.
Model short exchanges: 'How many apples would you like?' Then step back.
Add family items over the week, like baskets, aprons or food boxes from home cultures.
activities.safety: Wash real pumpkins and squash before play; they are for play, not eating.

activities.title: Pumpkin Roll and Carry
materials: Small pie pumpkins and large soft balls
steps: Outdoors, mark a start and finish line. Invite children to roll a pumpkin or ball along the path.
Try carrying a small pumpkin with two hands. Talk about heavy and light.
Load pumpkins into the wagon together and pull it to the 'farm stand'.
Count how many trips it takes as a group.
activities.safety: Use small pumpkins children can lift easily; bend knees to lift; dress for the weather and add sun protection on bright days.

activities.title: Fall Harvest Walk
materials: Baskets or paper bags with handles
Clipboards with a simple picture checklist
steps: Walk the yard or neighbourhood looking for signs of fall: coloured leaves, gardens, fruit trees, squash on porches.
Invite children to tick off pictures on the checklist as they spot each item.
Collect fallen leaves only. Leave plants, berries and mushrooms where they are.
Back inside, look at the photos and talk about what you found.
activities.safety: Never eat anything found outside; no picking berries or mushrooms; keep walking ratios and hold hands near roads; dress for the weather; wash hands after.

activities.title: Inside a Pumpkin
materials: One large pumpkin with the top cut off by an adult
steps: Before opening, ask children to predict what is inside. Write their ideas down.
Invite children to reach in and scoop. Offer spoons to children who prefer not to touch.
Describe together: slimy, stringy, wet, cold. Add the words to the chart.
Compare predictions with what you found.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy list first (some children react to pumpkin or seeds); adults do all cutting; seeds stay in the bin, for children who no longer mouth objects, with supervision; wash hands before and after.

activities.title: Five Red Apples Chant
materials: Felt board with a tree shape
steps: Place five apples on the felt tree. Chant: 'Five red apples on the tree, one falls down for you and me.'
Invite a child to take one apple off. Count how many are left together.
Repeat down to zero. Let children lead and change the colour or the fruit.
Leave the felt board out so children can play the chant on their own.

activities.title: Thank-You Tree
materials: Large paper tree trunk on the wall
Photos of children and families (with consent)
steps: At circle, talk about the word thankful. Share something you are thankful for.
Invite each child to say or draw one thing they are thankful for. Write their exact words on a leaf.
Children add their leaf to the tree. Accept answers in any language.
Invite families to add leaves at pick-up through the week.

activities.title: Applesauce Together
materials: Apples peeled, cored and cut by an adult
Slow cooker or pot (adult use only, out of reach)
steps: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first. Wash hands together.
Show the cut apples, then cook them in a slow cooker or pot that stays out of children's reach.
Once fully cooled, invite children to take turns mashing the soft apples.
Taste together at snack. Talk about how the apples changed from hard to soft.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first; no nuts; adults cut and cook; children only handle fully cooled food; keep appliances and cords out of reach; offer an alternative snack.

activities.title: Apple Tree Seasons Story
materials: Picture book about an apple tree through the year
Four large cards: bare branches, blossoms, green leaves, apples
steps: Read a picture book about an apple tree through the seasons.
Show the four cards out of order. Invite children to put them in order and tell what happens.
Ask: 'What season is it now? How do you know?'
Children draw their own tree. Write their words beside their drawing.

activities.title: Sorting the Harvest
materials: Real apples, small pumpkins and large gourds (all bigger than a child's fist)
Picture labels for colour and size
steps: Pour the harvest items onto a mat. Ask children how they could sort them.
Follow the children's ideas: colour, size, bumpy and smooth.
Weigh a few items on the scale. Which is heaviest? Which is lightest?
Take a photo of each sort and post it with the children's words.
activities.safety: Wash produce first; gourds are for looking and sorting only, not eating; wash hands after.

activities.title: Leaf Pile Jump and Rake
steps: Check the area for sticks, rocks or anything sharp first.
Invite children to rake leaves into one big pile together.
Take turns jumping in, one or two at a time.
Rake it back up and talk about working as a team, like farmers at harvest.
activities.safety: Check leaf piles for sticks, rocks and hidden objects first; rakes stay pointed down; dress for the weather; wash hands after.

schedule.focus: Apples: looking, tasting, counting and painting.
Pumpkins and the harvest: what's inside, how heavy, and the market.
Gratitude and sharing: thanking the people who grow and cook our food.

observe: What words does each child use to describe taste, texture and weight?
Who counts with one-to-one touch, and who counts by rote?
How do children choose to sort the harvest, and do they explain their rule?
Who takes on roles at the market, and how do they negotiate turns at the register?
How does a child respond to the slimy feel of pumpkin: dive in, use a spoon, or watch?
What does each child say they are thankful for, and who do they name?
family: Invite families to share a fall or harvest food from their culture, by photo, recipe or a short visit.
Post the applesauce steps so families can make it at home with their child as the helper.
Ask families to add a leaf to the Thank-You Tree at pick-up.
Share a list of local farms, markets or community gardens, including free options like a walk to see a neighbourhood garden.
Send home the Five Red Apples chant in English and French, and invite families to teach it in their home language.
inclusion: Offer spoons, scoops or gloves for children who find wet or slimy textures hard; watching is a valid way to join in.
Use a visual sequence (wash, look, taste, clean up) for food activities.
Provide a seated station at table height for the pumpkin and sorting activities so children using mobility aids can join.
Accept pointing, sign or picture choices for taste-test votes.
Keep a quiet corner open during busy market play. Talk with families and any resource consultant about what works best for their child.

tips: Label the market stand and the harvest baskets in English and French.
Sing the Five Red Apples chant in French too: « Cinq pommes rouges dans l'arbre… ».
Invite families to share the words for apple and pumpkin in their home language and add them to the Thank-You Tree.
Accept answers in any language during taste tests and counting.

safety_notes: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first before any tasting or cooking; keep the room nut-free and offer alternatives.
Adults do all cutting and cooking; children handle only cooled food and wash hands before and after.
Apple and pumpkin seeds are small: use them only with children who no longer mouth objects, with supervision, and count them back in.
Outdoors, never eat anything found outside; collect leaves only.

title: Community Helpers
summary: Children meet the people who keep their neighbourhood running, from mail carriers and firefighters to grocers, librarians and the grown-ups at home. Through walks, visits and lots of pretend play, they learn that everyone can be a helper, including them.
big_questions: Who helps us in our neighbourhood, and how?
What tools do helpers use, and why?
How can we be helpers too?

goals.text: Children name several helpers in their neighbourhood and describe what they do.
Children take on roles in pretend play, sharing ideas and materials with friends.
Children see their own families' work and contributions valued in the room.
Children learn simple safety habits: holding hands on walks, stopping at curbs, knowing who can help.
Children help with real classroom jobs and feel proud of their contribution.

activities.title: Who Helps Us? Photo Talk
materials: Real photos of local helpers (many genders, ages and backgrounds)
steps: Show one photo at a time. Ask: 'What is this person doing? How do they help?'
Write children's words beside each photo.
Ask who they have seen helping in their own neighbourhood.
Post the chart at child height and add to it all unit long.

activities.title: Neighbourhood Helper Walk
materials: Picture checklist (mailbox, fire hydrant, store, bus, library)
First aid kit and emergency contacts
steps: Before leaving, practise walking with a partner and stopping at every curb.
Walk a planned, short route. Look for helpers and the things they use.
Children tick their checklists as they spot each item. Wave and say hello to helpers you meet.
Back inside, look at photos and add new helpers to the chart.
activities.safety: Plan the route ahead; keep ratios with an educator at the front and back; hold hands near roads; stop at every curb; dress for the weather and use sun protection.

activities.title: Animal Clinic
steps: Set up a clinic with a waiting room and an exam table.
Invite children to bring a 'sick' stuffed animal and tell what is wrong.
Model caring words: 'You're safe. I'll be gentle.' Then let children lead.
Talk about real visits to the doctor or vet and how it felt.

activities.title: Fire Station Pretend Play
materials: Large box painted as a fire truck
Short pool noodle sections for hoses
Picture of a real firefighter in gear
steps: Show the photo of a firefighter in full gear. Talk about how the mask and helmet can look different, but it's a helper.
Invite children to dress up and 'drive' to help.
Practise the helper rule: if we see fire, we tell a grown-up right away.
Let the play follow children's own stories.
activities.safety: Never use real lighters, matches or candles as props.

activities.title: Mail Carrier Letters
materials: Paper, envelopes and stickers for stamps
Cubbies labelled with names and photos
steps: Talk about what a mail carrier does. Show a real letter or card.
Invite children to draw or 'write' a letter to a friend or family member.
Help each child find a name on the cubbies and 'deliver' the letter.
Accept scribbles, pictures and letter shapes; write the child's words if asked.

activities.title: Delivery Truck Relay
steps: Outdoors, set up 'houses' with cones and picture signs.
Children load packages into wagons and deliver them to the matching house.
Count packages at each house when the route is done.
Switch roles: driver, loader, customer.
activities.safety: Use a flat, clear area; one rider per ride-on; dress for the weather and use sun protection.

activities.title: Helper Tool Match
materials: Large picture cards of tools (stethoscope, hose, mail bag, book, broom)
Real child-safe items when possible (empty mail bag, book, broom)
steps: Lay out the helper cards. Hold up one tool at a time.
Ask: 'Who would use this? Why?'
Let children match and explain. Some tools fit more than one helper; talk about that.
Leave the cards on a shelf for independent play.

activities.title: Bakery Playdough
steps: Talk about bakers: what they make and when they start work.
Invite children to roll, cut and shape 'breads' and 'cookies' for the bakery.
Count items onto trays and 'sell' them to friends.
Ask children about breads their families make or buy.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy list first; homemade playdough has wheat and salt, so use a gluten-free recipe if needed; playdough is not for eating; wash hands after.

activities.title: Family Helper Visit
materials: Space for a visitor to show tools or uniform
steps: Invite any family member to share their work, paid or unpaid, at home or outside it.
Help children prepare one question each before the visit.
Let the visitor show a tool or photo. Children ask their questions.
Afterwards, make a thank-you drawing together.
activities.safety: Follow your centre's visitor policy; any tools shown stay in the visitor's hands.

activities.title: Our Classroom Jobs
materials: Job chart with pictures (plant waterer, table wiper, line leader, book helper)
Child-sized cleaning cloths and watering can
steps: Talk about how our room has helpers too.
Introduce each job with a picture and a short demonstration.
Children place their name card on a job. Rotate jobs every few days.
Thank each helper at the end of the day by name.

activities.title: Build Our Neighbourhood
materials: Large paper or a rug map
steps: Look at photos from the walk. Ask: 'What was beside the library? Where is the bus stop?'
Invite children to build the neighbourhood with blocks on the map.
Add photos and figures. Name roads and places together.
Leave it up so children can keep building and playing.

activities.title: Thank-You Cards for Helpers
materials: Washable markers, crayons and paint sticks
steps: Choose a helper together: the mail carrier, the custodian, the cook or a local library.
Children make cards in their own way. Write their messages as they say them.
Deliver the cards in person on a walk or hand them to the helper at the centre.
Talk about how it feels to say and hear thank you.

activities.title: Red Light, Green Light Crossing
materials: Red, yellow and green circles on sticks
Crossing guard vest for the leader
steps: Draw a pretend road and crosswalk with chalk.
The leader holds up green (walk), yellow (slow) and red (stop).
Practise looking both ways and holding a partner's hand to cross.
Let children take turns being the crossing guard.
activities.safety: Play only in the fenced yard, never near a real road; dress for the weather and use sun protection.

schedule.focus: Helpers around us: who we see and where they work.
Helpers at work: pretending to be helpers and using their tools.
We are helpers too: family visits, classroom jobs and saying thank you.

observe: Which helpers does each child name first, and do they connect them to their own family?
How do children decide who plays which role, and how do they handle two children wanting the same one?
Who uses caring words or gentle hands in the animal clinic?
Which children stop at the curb and look both ways without a reminder?
How does each child approach writing a letter: drawing, scribbles, letter shapes or their name?
Who takes pride in a classroom job, and how do they show it?
family: Invite families to share their work or volunteer roles, in person, by photo or with a short note.
Ask families to point out helpers on the way to the centre and tell their child what each helper does.
Send home a blank card for children to make a thank-you for someone who helps their family.
Share a list of free community places to visit, like the local library or a fire station open house.
Suggest a simple home job a child can do, like setting out spoons or feeding a pet.
inclusion: Use photo cards of real helpers and tools so every child can point, sign or name.
Offer a role card with one picture for children who need help joining pretend play.
Prepare children ahead for visitors or walks with a short picture story; offer ear defenders if busy streets are loud.
Plan walk routes with smooth sidewalks and curb cuts for children using mobility aids or strollers.
Give extra time and first/then language for transitions in and out of dramatic play. Check in with families and any resource consultant about routines that help.

tips: Label the dramatic play props in English and French (le casque, la lettre, le pain).
Name both the masculine and feminine forms of each job so all children see themselves.
Ask families how they say 'helper' and the names of their jobs in their home language.
Accept answers in any language when children name helpers and tools.

safety_notes: Walks need a planned route, full ratios, a first aid kit and emergency contacts; hold hands near roads.
Follow your centre's visitor policy; visitors' tools stay in their hands.
Check every child's allergy list before playdough and food-themed play; nothing in play is for eating.
Keep props large and sturdy; no real lighters, matches, medicines or sharp tools in dramatic play.

title: Winter Animals
summary: How do Ontario animals get through the cold? Children explore animals that sleep through winter, animals that fly away and animals that stay and adapt. They look for tracks in the snow, test how fur and fat keep animals warm, and move like bears, geese and hares.
big_questions: Where do animals go when it gets cold?
How do animals stay warm in winter?
What clues do animals leave in the snow?

goals.text: Children describe how some animals sleep, some travel and some stay active in winter.
Children investigate how fur, feathers and fat keep animals warm through simple hands-on tests.
Children enjoy active outdoor winter play and learn to dress for the cold.
Children look after living things by watching birds and animals gently and from a distance.
Children share winter stories and animals from their families' experiences.

activities.title: Who Sleeps All Winter?
materials: Picture book about animals in winter
Photos of a black bear, groundhog, chipmunk, Canada goose, red fox and snowshoe hare
Three picture labels: sleep, travel, stay
steps: Read a short picture book about animals in winter.
Show each photo. Ask: 'What do you think this animal does when it snows?'
Sort photos under sleep, travel or stay together. Children can change their minds.
Leave the sort on the wall to add to all unit.

activities.title: Bear Den Hideaway
materials: Table or frame draped with heavy blankets
steps: Build a cozy den with the children. Talk about why bears need a safe place to sleep.
Invite two or three children at a time to rest, read or snuggle a bear in the den.
Use the den as a calm-down space. Show how slow 'bear breaths' help us feel calm.
Practise waking up slowly in spring: stretch, yawn and crawl out.
activities.safety: Keep blankets draped over a sturdy frame, never over children; keep the den open on one side so educators can see in.

activities.title: Track Detectives
materials: Large laminated track cards (squirrel, rabbit, bird, dog, deer)
steps: After a fresh snowfall, look for tracks in the yard or a nearby park.
Compare tracks to the cards. Ask: 'Big or small? Hopping or walking? Where did it go?'
Follow a trail a short way and wonder together about the animal's story.
Photograph tracks to look at again inside.
activities.safety: Dress in warm, dry layers; check fingers, toes and cheeks often; look but don't touch animal droppings; never eat snow or anything found outside; wash hands after.

activities.title: Make Our Own Tracks
materials: Fresh snow or a tray of homemade playdough
Large plastic animals with clear feet
steps: Outside, invite children to walk, hop and crawl in fresh snow to make different tracks.
Look back: whose tracks are biggest? Which are hopping tracks?
Indoors on cold days, press large animal figures into playdough instead.
Play a guessing game: one child makes tracks, others guess the animal.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy list before playdough (wheat); dress for the cold and come in if anyone is wet or shivering.

activities.title: Bird Feeder Watch
materials: Tray bird feeder outside a window
Bird photo cards (chickadee, blue jay, cardinal, junco)
steps: An adult fills the feeder with nut-free seed. Children watch from the window.
Each day, children make a tally mark for every bird they see.
Match birds to the photo cards. Notice colours, sizes and sounds.
Count the tallies at the end of the week. Which bird visited most?
activities.safety: Use birdseed with no peanuts or tree nuts; adults handle seed; children watch from inside and wash hands if they touch the feeder.

activities.title: Fly South Like Geese
materials: Open space outdoors or in the gym
Picture of geese flying in a V
steps: Show the picture of geese in a V. Talk about how geese take turns at the front.
Children 'fly' in a V with arms out, following a leader from north to south.
Switch leaders often. Add honking and a rest stop on a 'pond'.
Fly back north to show spring.
activities.safety: Use a clear, open space; dress for the weather; leave room between children.

activities.title: Blubber Mitt Test
steps: An adult makes a 'blubber mitt': shortening sealed between two gloves, cuff taped closed.
Invite children to dip one bare finger in ice water for a moment. How does it feel?
Now try a hand in the blubber mitt. Compare: colder or warmer?
Talk about how fat and fur help seals, bears and other animals stay warm.
activities.safety: With an educator within arm's reach of the water; short dips only; dry hands right away; use non-latex gloves; tip out water when done.

activities.title: Fur, Feathers or Scales?
materials: Large fabric squares (faux fur, fleece, felt, shiny fabric)
Photos of animals with fur, feathers and scales
Feely bag made from a pillowcase
steps: Pass around the fabric squares. Describe each one: soft, fluffy, smooth, slippery.
Match each fabric to an animal photo.
Play a feely game: reach into the pillowcase and guess the fabric.
Ask: 'Which one would keep you warmest outside today?'

activities.title: Snowy Owl Collage
materials: Torn white tissue and paper scraps
steps: Look at photos of snowy owls. Notice the white feathers and yellow eyes.
Invite children to tear paper and glue it onto the owl however they like.
Add eyes with paint or crayons.
Write each child's words about their owl beside it.

activities.title: Our Winter Animals Book
materials: Photos from track walks and the feeder
Hole punch and binder rings (adult use)
steps: Invite each child to draw a favourite winter animal.
Ask: 'Where is your animal now? What is it doing?' Write their words on the page.
Add photos from the unit. An adult binds the pages.
Read the class book at circle and keep it in the book corner.

activities.title: Five Sleepy Chipmunks
materials: Five large chipmunk puppets or felt cut-outs
steps: Chant: 'Five sleepy chipmunks, snug in their bed. One went to sleep and lay down its head.'
Move one chipmunk into the burrow each time. Count how many are still awake.
Let children take turns moving chipmunks and leading the chant.
Try it with bears, frogs or groundhogs too.

activities.title: Ice Animal Rescue
materials: Large plastic animals frozen in ice blocks (made overnight in containers)
steps: Show the frozen animals. Ask: 'How can we help them get out?'
Offer warm water, spoons and droppers. Let children test their ideas.
Talk about what melts the ice faster.
Count the rescued animals and give them a warm 'den' on a towel.
activities.safety: With an educator within arm's reach of the water; use warm (not hot) water; animals must be larger than a choke tube; tip out water when done.

activities.title: Hide Like a Snowshoe Hare
materials: Photos of a snowshoe hare in summer and winter
Snowy yard or open play space
steps: Show both hare photos. Ask: 'Why do you think its coat changes?'
Hide white and brown fabric squares in the snow. Which are harder to find?
Play hide and seek: hares crouch still; the fox counts and looks.
Talk about how colour helps animals stay safe.
activities.safety: Hide only in open, visible areas of the fenced yard; dress in warm, dry layers; check for cold fingers and toes.

schedule.focus: Sleeping through winter: bears, chipmunks and groundhogs.
Travelling and staying warm: geese, birds, fur and fat.
Clues in the snow: tracks, hiding and telling animal stories.

observe: How does each child explain where an animal goes in winter? Do they change their ideas?
Who notices differences in track size or pattern, and what words do they use?
Which children use the bear den to calm down, and how long do they stay?
How do children test ideas during the ice rescue: try one way, or many?
Who counts the bird tallies, and do they compare more and less?
How do children manage their own winter clothing, and who helps a friend?
family: Invite families to look for tracks on the way home and share a photo.
Share how to make a simple ice block with a toy inside for a home ice rescue.
Ask families to share winter animal stories or animals from where they grew up.
Post a winter clothing checklist with pictures to help with dressing routines.
Send home the Five Sleepy Chipmunks chant in English and French.
inclusion: Provide a picture sequence for getting dressed for outdoors, and allow extra time.
Offer the blubber mitt and ice play with spoons or droppers for children who prefer not to touch cold.
Keep a cleared, packed path in the snow so children using mobility aids can join track walks.
Use the bear den as a quiet space with a sign or picture children can use to ask for it.
Use signs or gestures for animal names and movements. Talk with families and any resource consultant about cold sensitivity and comfort needs.

tips: Label the sleep, travel and stay sort in English and French.
Chant Five Sleepy Chipmunks in French too: « Cinq petits tamias dans leur lit… ».
Invite families to share animal names in their home language for the class book.
Accept answers in any language during track detective walks.

safety_notes: Dress in warm, dry layers; check fingers, toes and cheeks often and follow your centre's cold-weather policy.
Never eat snow or anything found outside; look at animal signs but don't touch droppings.
Water and ice play always with an educator within arm's reach; tip out water when done.
Use nut-free birdseed and check allergy lists before playdough.

title: Seeds and Growing Things
summary: Children plant, watch and care for bean seeds, sunflowers and herbs over four weeks. They predict, measure and record growth, look for seeds outside and learn what plants need. Caring for living things builds patience, responsibility and a sense of wonder.
big_questions: What is inside a seed, and what does it need to grow?
How can we tell our plants are growing?
How do we take care of living things?

goals.text: Children predict, observe and describe how a seed changes as it grows.
Children measure and compare plant growth with simple non-standard units.
Children take turns caring for plants and feel proud of their role.
Children use their hands and bodies to dig, plant, pour and move outdoors.
Children record what they see through drawing, talk and photos.
Children learn about plants and gardens that matter to their families.

activities.title: What's Inside a Seed?
materials: Large untreated bean seeds soaked overnight
steps: Show dry and soaked beans. Ask: 'What changed? Why?'
With an adult, gently peel a soaked bean and open it. Look for the tiny plant inside.
Children draw what they see.
Collect every bean at the end and count them back into the container.
activities.safety: Bean seeds are not for eating or mouthing; for children who no longer mouth objects, with supervision; use untreated seeds; wash hands after.

activities.title: Bean in a Window Cup
steps: Each child folds a damp paper towel into a cup.
An adult helps tuck two bean seeds between the towel and the cup wall.
Label each cup with a name and photo. Place by the window.
Check daily. Spray to keep the towel damp and talk about changes.
activities.safety: Bean seeds are not for eating or mouthing; an adult hands out and places seeds; untreated seeds only; wash hands after.

activities.title: Planting Day
materials: Sunflower seeds and herb seeds (basil, parsley)
steps: Outside, fill pots with soil together. Talk about how it feels and smells.
Poke a hole with a finger. Drop in seeds; an adult helps count them out.
Cover with soil and water gently.
Label each pot with a picture of the plant and the planter's name.
activities.safety: Seeds and soil are not for eating or mouthing; adults hand out seeds; use plain potting soil without added fertilizer; sun protection; wash hands after.

activities.title: Plant Care Crew
steps: Introduce the care crew jobs with pictures.
Each day, two children water and check the plants.
Ask: 'Is the soil dry or wet? Does it need water today?'
Thank the crew at circle and add a sticker to the chart.

activities.title: How Tall Now?
materials: Large linking cubes or unit blocks
steps: Hold a paper strip beside a plant. Mark its height and add the date.
Measure with linking cubes: 'How many cubes tall?'
Glue each strip onto the growth chart in order.
Compare this week's strip with last week's. Taller or shorter?

activities.title: Garden Centre Pretend Play
steps: Set up a garden centre in dramatic play with the children's help.
Invite roles: gardener, shopper, cashier.
Model asking: 'What will you grow? Where will you plant it?'
Add children's own ideas, like a delivery truck or a flower shop.

activities.title: Seed Hunt Walk
materials: Picture cards: maple keys, dandelion puffs, pine cones
steps: Walk the yard or park looking for seeds plants make.
Blow a dandelion puff and watch the seeds fly. How do seeds travel?
Collect a few fallen maple keys and large pine cones.
Back inside, sort and display your finds.
activities.safety: Never eat anything found outside; no picking berries, mushrooms or unknown plants; sun protection; wash hands after.

activities.title: Grow Like a Seed
steps: Children curl up small like seeds in the soil.
Pretend to get rain and sun. Slowly push up roots and a stem.
Stretch tall, open arms like leaves, sway in the wind with scarves.
End by curling up again to rest.

activities.title: Sunflower Painting
materials: Yellow, brown and green washable paint
steps: Look closely at the sunflower. Count petals together and notice the centre.
Invite children to paint their own sunflower in any way.
Ask about their colours and shapes, and write their words beside the art.
Display the art near the real plants.

activities.title: Herb Smell Station
steps: Invite children to gently rub a leaf and smell their fingers.
Ask: 'What does it remind you of? Do you like it?'
Match the smell bowls to the plants with eyes closed.
Talk about herbs families use in cooking.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first; this is a smelling activity, not tasting; wash hands after.

activities.title: Root Watch
steps: Look at the roots through the clear cups. Which way do they grow?
Turn a cup on its side. Predict what the roots will do over a few days.
Draw the roots and take a daily photo.
Compare drawings and photos at the end of the week.

activities.title: Big Dig
materials: Garden bed or large dirt area
steps: Check the digging area first for sharp objects.
Invite children to dig, fill buckets and move soil in the wheelbarrow.
Notice what you find: worms, roots, rocks.
Help prepare a bed for planting together.
activities.safety: Check the area for sharp objects and animal waste first; tools point down; soil is not for eating; wash hands after; sun protection.

activities.title: Seed Sorting Tray
materials: Large seeds: lima beans, sunflower seeds in shells, peach pits (washed and dried)
Photo cards of seeds for younger children
steps: Invite children to look at each kind of seed and describe it.
Sort seeds by size, colour or shape using tongs and the muffin tin.
Count how many are in each cup.
Offer the large photo cards to sort instead for children who still mouth objects.
activities.safety: For children who no longer mouth objects, with supervision; seeds are not for eating; count all seeds back in and store them out of reach; check allergy lists for sunflower.

activities.title: Our Garden Journal
steps: Each week, add a page about the plants.
Invite children to draw and tell what they see. Write their exact words.
Add a photo and the date.
Read the journal together to see how the plants changed.

activities.title: Light or Dark Test
materials: A cupboard and a sunny window
steps: Ask: 'Do plants need light?' Record each child's guess on the chart.
Put one plant in a dark cupboard and one in the window. Water both the same.
Check both every two days. Talk about colour and height.
Compare with the predictions, then move the dark plant back to the light.

activities.title: Gentle Worm Watch
materials: Damp soil area or garden bed
steps: Look for worms after rain or while digging.
Use gentle hands or a scoop to place a worm in the bug viewer with damp soil.
Observe: how does it move? Talk about how worms help the soil.
Return the worm to where you found it within a few minutes.
activities.safety: Handle worms gently and return them quickly; keep the viewer damp and out of the sun; wash hands after.

activities.title: Family Plant Stories
materials: Photos families send of plants, gardens or foods they grow
steps: Invite families ahead to share a photo of a plant, garden or herb they love.
At circle, each child shows and tells about their photo.
Find places on the map if families shared where a plant grows.
Post the photos on a 'Plants in Our Families' board.

schedule.focus: Seeds: what they look like, what's inside and where we find them.
Planting: soil, pots and starting our garden.
Caring and measuring: watering, checking and tracking growth.
Celebrating growth: art, stories and sharing our garden.

observe: What does each child predict will happen to a seed, and how do they explain it?
Who notices small changes in the bean cups first, and what words do they use?
How do children measure: do they line up the strip from the soil or the pot's edge?
Who takes care of plants without being asked, and how do they show gentleness?
How do children treat the worms, and do they remind each other to be gentle?
What do children's drawings show about roots, stems and leaves over time?
family: Invite families to share a photo of a plant, garden or herb they grow or love.
Send home a bean cup or a spare seedling to grow, with simple care pictures.
Suggest a seed hunt in the kitchen: seeds inside an apple, pepper or tomato (adults cut).
Share a list of local community gardens or library seed programs, which are often free.
Ask families how to say 'seed', 'plant' and 'flower' in their home language.
inclusion: Offer gloves, scoops and large-handled tools for children who dislike soil or need a bigger grip.
Use raised pots or a table-height planter so children using mobility aids can plant and water.
Use photo cards for seed sorting so every child can join, including those still mouthing.
Post a visual daily care routine (check, water, measure) with pictures.
Give extra time for waiting and turn-taking; use a first/then card. Talk with families and any resource consultant about what supports their child.

tips: Label each pot and plant in English and French.
Use French words during the Grow Like a Seed movement: « Je suis une petite graine… je pousse ! ».
Invite families to add plant names in their home language to the family plants board.
Accept predictions and garden journal words in any language.

safety_notes: Seeds, beans and soil are not for eating or mouthing; use untreated seeds; small seeds only for children who no longer mouth objects, with supervision; count seeds back in.
Grow only non-toxic plants such as beans, sunflowers and common herbs; never eat anything found outside.
Check every child's allergy list for herbs and sunflower seeds; wash hands after soil, seeds and plants.
Outdoors, use sun protection and check digging areas for sharp objects and animal waste.

title: Water and Weather
summary: Spring brings rain, puddles, wind and sunshine. Children track the weather, splash in puddles, catch rain and watch water disappear. Simple tests help them wonder where water goes, and talk about the weather helps them get ready for each day.
big_questions: Where does rain come from, and where does it go?
How can we tell what the weather is today?
What happens to a puddle on a sunny day?

goals.text: Children observe and name types of weather and record them on a chart.
Children investigate water by catching, pouring and watching it evaporate.
Children choose clothing for the weather and enjoy active play outside in all conditions.
Children share weather words, songs and stories from their families and work together on group tasks.

activities.title: Weather Watchers Chart
materials: Large weather chart with picture cards (sun, cloud, rain, wind)
Name cards for the weather helper
steps: Each morning, the weather helper looks out the window and reports.
Ask: 'What do you see? What do you hear? How does the air feel?'
The helper places a picture card on today's day.
Count the sunny and rainy days at the end of the week.

activities.title: Puddle Jumping
materials: Rain gear: boots, splash pants, raincoats
steps: Dress for rain together. Check puddles for depth and hidden objects first.
Invite children to jump, stomp and splash.
Measure a puddle's depth with a stick. Ask: 'Deep or shallow?'
Change into dry clothes and talk about how it felt.
activities.safety: Check puddles first and avoid deep water, roads and drains; with an educator within arm's reach of any deeper water; no outdoor play during thunder or lightning; change wet clothes after.

activities.title: Catch the Rain
materials: Tape marks or stickers at even heights
steps: Set the container outside in an open spot before rain.
After the rain, check together. Which tape mark did the water reach?
Record the level on the sheet with a sticker or drawing.
Compare days: more rain or less rain?
activities.safety: Use plastic, not glass; tip out the water after checking so it doesn't sit; no outdoor play during thunder or lightning.

activities.title: Where Did the Water Go?
materials: A sunny windowsill and a shady shelf
steps: Fill two cups to the same level. Mark the line with tape.
Place one in the sun and one in the shade. Ask children to predict.
Check every day and mark the new level.
Talk about the word evaporate: the water went into the air.
activities.safety: Place cups out of reach so they aren't spilled; wipe up spills right away.

activities.title: Painting with Water
steps: Outdoors on a warm day, invite children to 'paint' the fence or pavement with water.
Make big marks, shapes and names.
Watch what happens to the marks. Where do they go?
Compare a sunny spot and a shady spot.
activities.safety: With an educator within arm's reach of the buckets; small amounts of water only; tip out water when done; sun protection.

activities.title: Rain Cloud Jar
materials: Large clear plastic jar of water
White foam (shaving cream) handled by an educator only
Washable food colouring mixed with water in cups
steps: An educator puts a layer of foam 'cloud' on top of the water.
Children add coloured water drops onto the cloud with droppers.
Watch until the 'rain' falls through. Ask: 'What made it rain?'
Talk about real clouds getting heavy with water.
activities.safety: Only the educator handles the foam; keep it away from eyes and mouths; with an educator within arm's reach of the water; tip out water when done.

activities.title: Make a Rainstorm
materials: Drums or shakers made by adults and sealed
steps: Sit in a circle. Start with soft finger taps for a light drizzle.
Add rubbing hands, patting knees, then stomping for a big storm.
Slow down to a drizzle again, then quiet.
Let children lead the storm and add shakers.
activities.safety: Any homemade shakers are sealed with lid glued and taped.

activities.title: Sink or Float
materials: Large objects: cork board piece, wooden block, large rock, plastic lid, metal spoon
Two sorting trays labelled sink and float
steps: Hold up each object. Children predict: sink or float?
Test it in the water. Sort onto the right tray.
Talk about surprises. Why do you think it floated?
Invite children to find other safe objects to test.
activities.safety: With an educator within arm's reach of the water; all objects bigger than a choke tube; tip out water when done; wipe floors to prevent slips.

activities.title: Dress for the Weather
materials: Doll clothes: raincoat, boots, sun hat, mittens, scarf
steps: Pick a weather card. Ask: 'What should Teddy wear today?'
Children choose and dress the teddy.
Check today's weather chart and talk about what we need to wear outside.
Practise one real step together, like zipping a raincoat.

activities.title: Rainy Day Stories
materials: Picture books about rain and weather
steps: Read a picture book about a rainy day.
Collect weather words: drizzle, pour, splash, puddle, thunder.
Ask children to share a rainy-day memory. Write their words.
Create a class rainy-day story together.

activities.title: Wind Watchers
materials: Short crepe-paper streamers tied to the fence
Outdoor pinwheels mounted in the garden
steps: Look at the streamers. Ask: 'Is the wind blowing? Which way?'
Run with scarves and feel the wind push and pull.
Check the streamers and pinwheels at different times of day.
Add a wind card to the weather chart.
activities.safety: Tie streamers to the fence, never to children; remove them after play; dress for the weather.

schedule.focus: Rain and puddles: watching, catching and splashing.
Where water goes: evaporation, wind and our weather chart.

observe: What words does each child use to describe the weather and how it feels?
Who notices the water level changing in the evaporation cups, and how do they explain it?
How do children predict sink or float, and do they change their ideas after testing?
Who chooses clothing to match the weather, and who needs support?
How do children take turns leading the rainstorm, and how do others follow?
family: Invite families to send a photo of a puddle or weather at home and post them on a weather wall.
Share how to leave a cup of water on a windowsill at home and check it each day.
Ask families for weather words and songs in their home language.
Remind families about spare dry clothes and rain gear, and share a list of low-cost or donated options if available.
Suggest a family weather walk: look, listen and feel the air together.
inclusion: Offer rain gear and towels nearby; let children who dislike being wet watch puddle play or use a long-handled scoop.
Use picture cards for weather reports so every child can take a turn as weather helper.
Provide a calm space if loud rainstorm sounds are overwhelming; offer quiet tapping as a choice.
Plan outdoor spots with level ground for children using mobility aids.
Give time to process predictions and accept pointing or sign. Check in with families and any resource consultant about sensory needs.

tips: Add French words to the weather chart cards: « Il pleut », « Il fait soleil », « Il vente ».
Ask the weather helper to report in English, French or a home language.
Label rain gear hooks in both languages.
Invite families to share a short weather rhyme in their home language.

safety_notes: All water play with an educator within arm's reach; tip out water when done and wipe up spills.
Check puddles before play; stay away from deep water, drains and roads; no outdoor play during thunder or lightning.
Dress for the weather, use sun protection on bright days and change wet clothes promptly.
Use plastic containers only; keep foam and food colouring away from eyes and mouths.

title: Builders and Construction
summary: Children build towers, bridges and whole cities with blocks, boxes and large loose parts. They try out tools, draw plans and work together on big outdoor projects. Building invites problem solving, early math and teamwork, and lets children feel strong and capable.
big_questions: How can we make our buildings tall and strong?
What tools do builders use, and what do they do?
How can we build something big together?

goals.text: Children test ways to make structures tall, wide and stable, and try again when they fall.
Children use shape, size and counting words while building and measuring.
Children share materials and ideas to build together.
Children lift, carry and move large materials with growing strength and control.
Children plan and show their building ideas through drawings, talk and photos.

activities.title: Tall Tower Challenge
steps: Ask: 'How tall can we build a tower before it falls?'
Invite children to build. Notice what they put on the bottom.
Measure the tower against a child or the wall chart.
When it falls, ask: 'What could we try next time?'
activities.safety: Keep towers below children's shoulder height; build away from walkways; stand back when it falls.

activities.title: Bridge Builders
steps: Lay the blue fabric down. Ask: 'How can the cars get across?'
Invite children to build bridges with blocks and cardboard.
Test each bridge with a toy car. Does it hold?
Try making it longer or stronger.

activities.title: Construction Site Pretend Play
steps: Set up a construction site with children's help.
Invite roles: builder, crane operator, foreman, inspector.
Model asking: 'What are we building today?' Then step back.
Add children's ideas, like a lunch break or a delivery truck.

activities.title: Tool Detectives
materials: Large photo cards of real tools
steps: Show each tool card. Ask: 'What does this tool do?'
Children find the matching toy tool and act out how it works.
Play a feely box game: reach in and guess the tool by touch.
Talk about tools families use at home.

activities.title: Box City
steps: Show the boxes. Ask: 'What could we build for our city?'
Children tape, stack and paint boxes into houses, shops and towers.
An adult cuts any doors or windows children ask for.
Arrange the city together and name the streets.
activities.safety: Adults do all cutting; remove staples from boxes first.

activities.title: Big Loose Parts Build
materials: Large bottle caps (for children who no longer mouth objects, with supervision)
steps: Set out the loose parts with no instructions.
Invite children to build anything they like.
Ask: 'Tell me about your building. How did you make it stay up?'
Photograph the creations and keep the materials out all week.
activities.safety: Keep small loose parts like bottle caps only for children who no longer mouth objects, with supervision, and count them back in; check planks for splinters.

activities.title: Shape Builders
materials: Blocks in different shapes (cubes, cylinders, arches, triangles)
Photos of buildings with clear shapes
steps: Look at building photos. Find squares, triangles and arches.
Invite children to build using a shape card as a guide.
Count the shapes in each building.
Ask: 'Which shape is good for the bottom? Which for the roof?'

activities.title: Outdoor Big Build
materials: Large hollow blocks or plastic crates
steps: Outside, invite children to build a fort, a road or a house together.
Help children plan: where will the door go?
Encourage teamwork: 'This plank is heavy. Who can help?'
Play in the build, then take it down together.
activities.safety: Keep builds low to the ground; no climbing on stacked crates above knee height; check planks for splinters; dress for the weather and use sun protection.

activities.title: Wagon Haulers
steps: Set up a 'supply yard' and a 'building site' outdoors.
Children load blocks into wagons and haul them across.
Count the loads together. Which load was heaviest?
Use the blocks to build at the site.
activities.safety: Use a flat, clear area; lift with bent knees; no riding in wagons; dress for the weather.

activities.title: Builder Blueprints
steps: Show photos of real building plans. Talk about why builders draw plans first.
Invite children to draw a plan for something they want to build.
Write their words on the plan.
Children build from their plan, then compare the two.

activities.title: Builders Song and Story
materials: Picture book about building or construction
Picture cards of building actions (dig, hammer, lift, pour)
steps: Read a picture book about building.
Sing a made-up song to a familiar tune: 'This is the way we hammer the nails.'
Add a verse for each action card children choose.
Invite children to act out each action.

activities.title: Pound and Tap
materials: Wooden pounding bench with large pegs
steps: Show how to tap gently and strongly with a mallet.
Invite children to pound pegs into the bench.
Press large pegs into playdough and tap them in.
Talk about how hammering feels and how loud it is.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy list before playdough (wheat); one child per bench; use toy mallets only.

activities.title: Measure Our Building
steps: Choose a building. Ask: 'How tall is it? How can we find out?'
Measure with linking cubes, blocks or a paper strip.
Record the number on the sheet.
Compare buildings: taller, shorter, the same?

activities.title: When It Falls Down
steps: Talk about how it feels when a building falls: frustrated, sad, surprised.
Practise calm-down ideas: deep breath, ask for help, try again.
Agree on building rules together: we only knock down our own buildings.
Celebrate trying again and help each other rebuild.

schedule.focus: Blocks and towers: building tall and strong.
Tools and builders: how builders work, plan and use tools.
Big projects together: box cities, loose parts and outdoor builds.

observe: What does each child do when a building falls: rebuild, change plans, ask for help?
Who uses words like taller, wider, heavier and on top of?
How do children share materials and roles during big builds?
Which children plan before building, and which plan as they go?
How does a child's blueprint compare to what they build?
Who lifts and carries with care for their own and others' safety?
family: Invite families to send photos of buildings in their neighbourhood or where they grew up.
Suggest building at home with clean recycled boxes, cans with smooth edges, and tape.
Ask families who build or fix things at work or home to share a photo or visit.
Share a free idea: walk past a construction site with your child and name the machines from a safe distance.
Send home the builders song so families can sing it together.
inclusion: Offer larger, lighter blocks and foam bricks for children who need an easier grip.
Build at table height and on the floor so every child can reach, including children using mobility aids.
Use a visual 'build, play, tidy' routine and a timer for turns.
Offer ear defenders during pounding and noisy builds, and a quiet building space.
Give extra processing time and first/then language at clean-up. Talk with families and any resource consultant about supports that work.

tips: Label the block shelf and tool bin in English and French.
Sing the builders song in French too: « Voilà comment on tape, on tape… ».
Ask families how to say 'build' and 'house' in their home language and add them to the box city.
Accept answers in any language when children describe their buildings.

safety_notes: Keep towers and outdoor builds low; no climbing on stacked materials; build away from walkways.
Small loose parts only for children who no longer mouth objects, with supervision; count them back in.
Use toy tools only; adults do all cutting; check boxes for staples and planks for splinters.
Check every child's allergy list before playdough.

title: Inventors and Engineers
summary: Children take on design challenges, find simple machines all around them and turn recycled materials into working inventions. Testing, failing and trying again builds persistence, teamwork and a real sense of 'I can figure this out.'
big_questions: How do machines help us do hard jobs?
What problem in our room could we solve with an invention?
What can we learn when a design doesn't work the first time?

goals.text: Children plan, build, test and improve their own designs.
Children notice and name simple machines (ramps, levers, wheels and axles, pulleys) in everyday life.
Children share ideas, take turns with tools and build on each other's plans.
Children manage frustration and keep going when a build falls apart.
Children explain their inventions through drawings, labels, models and talk.

activities.title: Inventor's Notebook
materials: Folded paper booklets or small notebooks
steps: Invite each child to make and name their own inventor's notebook.
Model a quick sketch with labels of something you built.
Offer time at the start or end of each day to draw plans, tests and changes.
Accept drawings, invented spelling, dictated words or any language.

activities.title: Cardboard Box Builders
steps: Set out boxes and ask, 'What could this become?'
Let children work alone or in small teams.
Help with tricky cuts; children do the planning and joining.
Leave builds up so they can return and add on.
activities.safety: Educators do any cutting of thick cardboard; remove staples and plastic film first.

activities.title: Outdoor Ramp Rally
materials: Planks, gutters or stiff cardboard ramps
Balls and toy cars of different sizes
steps: Prop ramps on the climber, a hill or crates at different heights.
Invite children to predict which ramp sends a ball farthest.
Mark landing spots with chalk and measure.
Ask, 'What could we change to make it go farther?'
activities.safety: Check ramps are stable; keep the run-out zone clear of running children. Sunscreen, hats and water on warm days.

activities.title: Simple Machine Hunt
materials: Picture cards: ramp, lever, wheel and axle, pulley, screw, wedge
steps: Show the picture cards and try each motion with your body.
Send small teams to hunt for machines around the centre.
Children tally or sketch what they find.
Gather to share: 'Which machine did we find the most?'

activities.title: Lever Launchers
materials: Blocks or thick markers as fulcrums
steps: Show how a ruler on a block lifts one end when you press the other.
Invite children to launch paper balls toward a basket.
Move the fulcrum and test again.
Talk about what changed and why.
activities.safety: Launch only soft paper balls, and only toward targets — never at people.

activities.title: Paper Bridge Challenge
materials: Toy cars or wooden blocks as weights
steps: Place two book stacks a ruler's length apart.
Challenge teams to build a paper bridge that holds a toy car.
Invite them to fold, roll or layer paper and test.
Count how many cars each design holds and share discoveries.

activities.title: Pulley Bucket Lift
materials: Small pulley or smooth bar on the climber
Light outdoor loose parts (pine cones, sticks)
steps: Set up the pulley with an educator at the station.
Invite children to lift loads up to the climber deck.
Try heavier and lighter loads; notice how it feels.
Ask teams to take turns as 'loader' and 'lifter'.
activities.safety: An educator stays at the pulley; rope never goes around necks or bodies, and it is taken down after play. No one stands under a raised load.

activities.title: Problem Spotters Meeting
steps: Ask, 'What bugs you in our room?' (e.g., markers rolling away, boots in a heap).
Record every idea on the chart.
Let children vote on problems to solve with an invention.
Form teams based on which problem each child chose.

activities.title: Recycled Invention Lab
steps: Remind teams of the problem they chose.
Invite them to sketch a plan in their notebooks first.
Build, test with the real problem and adjust.
Notice and name persistence: 'You tried three ways!'
activities.safety: Wash and sort recyclables first; no glass, cans with sharp rims, or containers that held cleaners.

activities.title: Ball Run Wall
materials: Ping-pong balls or soft foam balls
steps: Tape a starting tube high on the wall.
Invite children to add tubes so the ball reaches the floor.
Time runs or count how many turns the ball makes.
Encourage teams to join their runs into one long path.

activities.title: Take-Apart Table
materials: Pre-checked old items (wooden toys, hand egg beater, door latch, keyboard with cord removed)
steps: Show how to hold a screwdriver and turn 'lefty-loosey'.
Invite two or three children at a time to explore.
Sort parts into the muffin tin and guess what each one did.
Use the parts later for new inventions.
activities.safety: Educators check every item first: no batteries, glass, screens, springs under tension, sharp edges or cords. Safety glasses on; close supervision.

activities.title: Inventors' Showcase
steps: Help each child or team set up their invention with a name card.
Invite children to explain how it works to visitors or other groups.
Offer a 'test it yourself' station.
Celebrate the trying, not just what worked.

activities.title: Wind Car Grand Prix
steps: Invite children to build a car with a paper sail.
Take cars outside on a breezy day.
Test which sail shapes travel farthest.
Let children rebuild and race again.
activities.safety: Weather-appropriate clothing; sunscreen and hats in sun. Race on a flat, traffic-free surface.

activities.title: Wheel and Axle Garage
steps: Show a toy car and ask how the wheels turn.
Invite children to build a vehicle that rolls.
Test on a ramp and fix wobbly wheels.
Add the vehicles to the block area for play.

schedule.focus: What engineers do and the simple machines all around us
Machines that move, lift and launch
Inventing to solve real problems and sharing what we made

observe: What does a child do first when a build falls apart — fix it, ask for help, or walk away?
Who suggests ideas to the group, and how do others respond?
Which simple machines does a child name without prompting?
How does a child explain why one design worked better than another?
Who returns to the same challenge day after day, and what changes each time?
What do children's notebook drawings show about their planning?
family: Ask families to save clean boxes, tubes and lids for the invention lab.
Send home a 'machine hunt' list to try in the kitchen or on a walk.
Invite family members who build, fix or design things (in any job or hobby) to share a tool or story.
Share photos of builds-in-progress so families can ask about the process, not just the result.
Invite families to the Inventors' Showcase, in person or by photo and short note.
inclusion: Offer larger tools, chunky tape and pre-cut pieces for children who find fine motor work tiring.
Use a visual plan-build-test-fix card so every child can follow the steps.
Give children who prefer working alone their own build space alongside the group.
Accept plans by drawing, gesture, pointing or dictation as well as writing.
Set up stations at table and floor height so children using mobility aids can reach them.
Talk with families and any resource consultant about tools or supports that work at home.

tips: Label the invention stations and simple-machine cards in English and French.
Use a short French phrase for each step: 'On planifie, on construit, on essaie!'
Invite families to share the word for 'machine' or 'invent' in their home language.
Accept explanations in any language; restate them warmly in English and French.

safety_notes: Check every recycled and take-apart item first: no batteries (especially coin cells), glass, sharp edges, cords or containers that held chemicals.
In mixed-age groups, keep small parts and ping-pong balls away from children under 3.
Teach safe tool use and supervise closely; safety glasses at the take-apart table.
Outdoors: sunscreen, hats, water breaks and weather-appropriate clothing.

title: Ontario Wildlife and Habitats
summary: Children become field naturalists, exploring the animals, birds and habitats close to home as Ontario moves into fall. Nature walks, field notebooks and wildlife watching build curiosity, respect for living things and a sense of belonging to the land we share.
big_questions: Who lives in our neighbourhood besides people?
How do animals get ready for winter?
How can we be good neighbours to wildlife?

goals.text: Children observe local animals and habitats closely and record what they notice.
Children compare how different animals find food, shelter and stay safe.
Children treat living things gently and care for shared outdoor spaces.
continuum: Social: respect for others and the environment

goals.text: Children move, explore and feel confident outdoors in changing fall weather.
Children share discoveries with peers through talk, drawing, pretend play and models.

activities.title: Make a Field Notebook
materials: Paper folded and stapled into booklets
Elastic band to hold a pencil
steps: Show a naturalist's sketch and notes (from a book or your own).
Invite children to decorate their own field notebook cover.
Practise a quick 'look, sketch, label' with a leaf or pine cone.
Keep notebooks ready by the door for every walk.

activities.title: Habitat Walk
steps: Walk the yard or a nearby park slowly and quietly.
Stop at a tree, lawn, garden bed and puddle; ask, 'Who might live here?'
Invite children to sketch one habitat and its clues (holes, nests, chewed leaves).
Share findings back inside.
activities.safety: Weather-appropriate clothing. Look, don't pick: never touch wild animals, droppings or mushrooms, and never eat anything found outside. Check for ticks after long-grass areas.

activities.title: Bird Feeder Watch
materials: Simple feeder (clean milk carton or pine cone)
steps: Check every child's allergy list first; offer gloves.
Make a feeder together and hang it where children can see from a window.
Watch for 10 minutes each day and tally visitors by colour or type.
Compare counts across the week.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first; many birdseed mixes contain peanuts or tree nuts — use nut-free seed and no nut butters. Gloves for children with seed allergies; everyone washes hands after.

activities.title: Animal Track Detectives
materials: Life-size track cards (deer, raccoon, squirrel, goose, rabbit)
steps: Show track cards and invite children to guess who made them.
Press toy animal feet into dough or sand to make tracks.
Hide track cards around the room for others to find and match.
Look for real tracks in mud or sand outdoors.

activities.title: Who Lives Under the Log?
materials: Small spoon or soft brush for moving critters
steps: With an educator, gently roll a log or stone toward you.
Look for worms, sow bugs, beetles and spiders.
Move one critter into a bug viewer with a spoon for a short look.
Return every critter and roll the log back the way it was.
activities.safety: Educator rolls the log. Gentle hands; critters go back within minutes. Wash hands after. Never touch wild animals or droppings.

activities.title: Squirrel Stash Game
materials: Bean bags or soft balls as 'acorns'
steps: Explain that squirrels hide food to eat in winter.
Children race to carry 'acorns' one at a time to their nest.
Call 'Hawk!' and everyone freezes.
Try again with a bigger field and count stashes.
activities.safety: Clear the field of tripping hazards; dress for the weather and offer water breaks.

activities.title: Goose Migration Run
materials: Map of a migration route (simple drawing)
steps: Talk about Canada geese flying south in a V.
Children form small V-shaped flocks and 'fly' between lakes.
Rotate the leader to the back when the drum sounds, like real geese.
Rest and count how many lakes the flock reached.
activities.safety: Open, flat space; walk-then-jog pace for younger children; water break after.

activities.title: Habitat Diorama Boxes
materials: Fall leaves and twigs collected from the ground
steps: Invite children to choose an Ontario animal and its habitat (pond, forest, field, backyard).
Build the home in a box with natural and art materials.
Shape the animal from clay or draw it.
Label the box and share with a friend.

activities.title: Bark and Leaf Rubbings
materials: Tree picture guide (maple, oak, birch, pine)
steps: Visit three different trees in the yard or park.
Make a bark rubbing and a fallen-leaf rubbing from each.
Compare patterns and match leaves to the tree guide.
Add rubbings to field notebooks.
activities.safety: Use fallen leaves only; dress for the weather; no climbing trees during the activity.

activities.title: Our Wildlife Field Guide
materials: Field guide page templates (picture, name, home, food)
steps: Invite each child to choose an animal they saw or want to learn about.
Look it up together in picture books.
Fill a page with a drawing and a few words or dictated notes.
Bind pages into a class field guide for the reading corner.

activities.title: Who Am I? Animal Riddles
steps: Read a riddle: 'I have a striped tail and a mask. Who am I?'
Children guess, then show the photo.
Invite children to write or tell their own riddles.
Take turns stumping the group.

activities.title: Wildlife Wonder Wall
steps: Post the question, 'What do we wonder about animals near us?'
Children add questions, drawings and photos all unit long.
Revisit at circle and mark questions we answered.
Celebrate new discoveries together.

activities.title: Winter Den Pretend Play
materials: Blankets and a table or play tent
steps: Talk about animals that hibernate, migrate or stay active in winter.
Build a den together in the dramatic play area.
Invite children to play bear, chipmunk, goose or fox families.
Notice and name cooperation and turn-taking.

activities.title: Bird Call Listening Walk
steps: Find a quiet spot and sit still for two minutes.
Count how many different bird sounds you hear.
Invite children to copy calls (crow, chickadee, blue jay, goose).
Draw or note where each sound came from.
activities.safety: Weather-appropriate clothing; stay on paths; never touch birds, nests or feathers found on the ground.

schedule.focus: Habitats near us: who lives in our yard and park?
Birds and travellers: watching, listening and migrating
Getting ready for winter: tracks, dens and stashes

observe: How long can a child stay still and watch an animal or bird?
Which details does a child include in field notebook sketches?
How does a child handle a critter — and how do they remind others to be gentle?
What questions does a child ask about why animals do what they do?
Who uses new words like 'habitat', 'migrate' or 'hibernate' in play?
How do children share roles and ideas in den play?
family: Invite families to send a photo or drawing of an animal or bird they saw near home.
Share a simple 'backyard bird tally' sheet to try at a window over the weekend.
Ask families to share animal names, stories or songs from their home language or culture.
Suggest a family 'look, don't touch' walk to a local park or ravine.
Add picture books about Ontario animals, including books by Indigenous authors, to a lending basket.
inclusion: Choose accessible paths and viewing spots for children using mobility aids or strollers.
Offer binoculars, magnifiers and large-print photo cards for children who see better up close.
Provide ear defenders or a quieter spot for children who find outdoor noise overwhelming.
Let children record observations by photo, drawing, pointing or dictation.
Use a visual walk schedule (go, stop, look, sketch, return) and first/then language.
Talk with families and any resource consultant about what helps a child enjoy outdoor time.

tips: Label the bird chart and field guide pages in English and French.
Play 'Qui suis-je?' animal riddles in French on alternate days.
Invite families to add animal names in their home languages to the Wonder Wall.
Accept answers in any language and repeat them back in English and French.

safety_notes: Look, don't touch: no handling wild animals, birds, nests, feathers, droppings or dead animals; never pick or eat berries, mushrooms or plants found outside.
Birdseed and feeders: nut-free seed and no nut butters; check allergy lists; wash hands after.
Dress for fall weather, check for ticks after long grass, and keep head counts on every walk.
Critters are observed briefly in bug viewers and returned where they were found.

title: Healthy Bodies, Healthy Habits
summary: Children explore what helps their bodies and minds feel ready to play: moving, resting, drinking water, washing hands, eating a variety of foods and finding calm. Canada's Food Guide is used as a friendly guide to variety and eating together — all foods are welcome, and nobody's body is judged.
big_questions: What helps my body feel strong and ready to play?
How can I tell what my body and feelings need?
What can I do when I feel too wiggly, tired or upset?

goals.text: Children notice body signals (heartbeat, breathing, thirst, tiredness) and what they need.
Children practise self-care routines such as hand washing with growing independence.
Children enjoy active play indoors and out and try new ways to move.
Children name feelings and try calming strategies that work for them.
Children share family food traditions and eat together with curiosity and respect.

activities.title: Germ Detective Hand Wash
materials: A dab of washable paint as pretend germs
steps: Put a dab of washable paint on each child's palms and rub hands together.
Notice how 'germs' spread to everything you touch.
Wash with soap for 20 seconds while singing a song twice.
Check fingertips, thumbs and between fingers together.
activities.safety: Use non-toxic washable paint; skip paint for any child with skin sensitivities and use a dry demonstration instead.

activities.title: Snow Day Movement Circuit
materials: Spray bottles of coloured water to mark snow stations
steps: Set up stations: snow stomp, hoop hops, sled pull, snow angel, balance walk.
Children move through in pairs.
Stop to feel heartbeats and breathing after each round.
Invite children to design a new station.
activities.safety: Dress in layers, hats, mittens and dry boots; check for cold hands and red cheeks; come in early in extreme cold or wind chill. Food colouring water is for marking only.

activities.title: Heartbeat Detectives
materials: Chart paper for a class graph
steps: Show how to feel a heartbeat on the wrist or chest.
Count beats while sitting, then after a minute of jumping.
Graph 'slow' and 'fast' with stickers.
Ask, 'What helps your heart slow back down?'

activities.title: Food Guide Plate Collage
materials: Food pictures from flyers, including foods from many cultures
steps: Show a simple picture of a plate with vegetables and fruits, whole grains and protein foods, and water to drink.
Invite children to make a plate of foods they enjoy or eat at home.
