Talk about colours, textures and family favourites.
Display every plate; all family foods are welcome.
activities.safety: Talk about foods neutrally — no 'good' or 'bad' foods and no comments on body size or weight.

activities.title: Taste and Talk Snack
materials: Vegetables cut thin (cucumber rounds, pepper strips, steamed broccoli)
A dip that fits every child's list
steps: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first.
Wash hands together before handling food.
Invite children to serve themselves with tongs and describe crunch, colour and taste.
Let children decide whether and how much to taste — 'No thank you' is fine.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first. No peanuts or tree nuts; check dips for sesame and dairy and offer alternatives. Cut foods small or thin for younger children; children sit while eating.

activities.title: Breathing Buddies
steps: Children lie down with a soft toy on their belly.
Breathe in to lift the buddy, out to let it sink.
Try 'smell the flower, blow the candle' breaths.
Ask, 'How does your body feel now?'

activities.title: Feelings Weather Report
materials: Weather picture cards (sunny, cloudy, stormy, rainbow)
steps: Invite children to pick a weather card for how they feel inside.
Anyone who wants to can give a 'weather report' into the microphone.
Ask, 'What helps when it's stormy inside?' and list ideas.
Check in again later in the day.

activities.title: Body Battery Charts
materials: Picture book about rest or sleep
steps: Read a story about resting and recharging.
Invite children to colour a battery: full, half, low.
Draw or write what fills their battery (sleep, quiet time, a hug, water, play).
Share a few ideas and post the charts.

activities.title: Animal Yoga Adventure
steps: Tell a story where children travel through a forest.
Children make each animal pose as it appears (tree, cat, frog, bear, butterfly).
Invite children to lead a pose or invent one.
End with resting 'sleeping bear'.
activities.safety: Space mats apart; no one is pushed into a pose — children move within what feels comfortable.

activities.title: Mindful Snow Walk
steps: Walk slowly and quietly for a few minutes.
Notice five things you see, four you hear and three you feel.
Catch snowflakes on dark paper and look closely.
Talk about how the walk made your body feel.
activities.safety: Dress in layers with mittens and boots; shorten the walk in extreme cold; never eat snow or ice.

activities.title: Thirsty Body Tracker
materials: Each child's labelled water bottle or cup
Picture of body signals of thirst
steps: Ask, 'How does your body tell you it's thirsty?'
Children add a drop sticker each time they drink water.
Count drops as a group at the end of the day.
Talk about why we drink more after active play.
activities.safety: Children use only their own labelled bottle or cup; water is always available, not earned.

schedule.focus: Moving, growing and caring for our bodies
Rest, feelings and finding calm

observe: Which body signals can a child describe (tired, thirsty, heart racing)?
Which calming strategy does a child choose on their own when upset?
How independently does a child complete each hand-washing step?
How does a child try new movements — eager, cautious, watching first?
What family foods and traditions do children talk about with pride?
Does any child seem worried about food or their body, and who could I gently check in with?
family: Share the hand-washing song so families can sing it at home.
Invite families to send a photo or name of a favourite family dish for the collage wall.
Send home the 'smell the flower, blow the candle' breathing idea for bedtime or busy moments.
Share free winter activity ideas: snow walks, kitchen dance parties, indoor obstacle courses.
Ask families how their child likes to calm down, and use those ideas at the centre.
inclusion: Offer seated versions of yoga poses and movement stations for children who need them.
Use visual step cards at the sink and a mirror at child height.
Offer sensory alternatives to paint (dry demo, lotion) for children who dislike wet or messy hands.
Give feelings cards and gestures for children who prefer not to speak in a group.
Respect dietary needs, sensory food preferences and cultural or religious food practices without comment.
Talk with families and any resource consultant about routines, feeding supports or regulation strategies.

tips: Sing the hand-washing song in English and French.
Label the feelings weather cards in both languages.
Invite families to share food and body words in their home languages.
Accept feelings words in any language — the feeling matters more than the word.

safety_notes: Food activities: check every child's allergy and dietary list first, no peanuts or tree nuts, wash hands, cut food to size and seat children while eating.
Body-positive language only: no talk of diets, weight or 'good/bad' foods; all bodies and family foods are respected.
Winter outdoor play: layers, mittens, dry boots, frequent warm-up checks and shorter time in extreme cold.
Use non-toxic, washable materials and offer alternatives for children with skin sensitivities.

title: Story Makers
summary: Children become storytellers, puppeteers, comic artists, authors and actors. Telling stories out loud, building characters and making real books grows language, imagination and confidence — and every child's family stories have a place.
big_questions: What makes a story fun to hear again and again?
How many different ways can we tell the same story?
What stories does my family tell?

goals.text: Children tell and retell stories with a beginning, middle and end.
Children create characters and act them out through puppets, drama and movement.
Children make books and comics using pictures, symbols and words.
Children listen to, value and build on each other's stories, including family and cultural stories.
Children feel confident sharing their voice in small and large groups.

activities.title: Story Stones Circle
materials: Smooth stones painted with simple pictures (sun, fox, house, boat)
steps: Pass the basket; each child draws a stone.
Start a story; the next child adds a part using their stone.
Keep going around the circle until the story ends.
Ask, 'What was your favourite twist?'
activities.safety: In mixed-age rooms, keep stones away from children under 3.

activities.title: Sock Puppet Workshop
steps: Invite children to imagine a character: Who is it? What does it want?
Decorate a sock puppet for that character.
Give the puppet a name and a voice.
Have puppets introduce themselves to each other.
activities.safety: In mixed-age groups, keep small craft pieces away from children under 3; let glue dry before puppets are worn.

activities.title: Puppet Theatre Shows
materials: Puppet theatre or a table on its side with a cloth
steps: Help small groups plan a short show: who, where, what goes wrong, how it's fixed.
Rehearse once behind the theatre.
Perform for friends; audience claps for every show.
Invite performers to swap roles and try again.

activities.title: Comic Strip Studio
steps: Look at how comics show talking, thinking and action.
Invite children to plan a story in three panels: start, problem, ending.
Add speech bubbles with words, symbols or dictated text.
Post comics in a 'newsstand' for others to read.

activities.title: Make-Your-Own Book
materials: Hole punch and ribbon or stapler (educator use)
steps: Invite each child to choose a topic: a made-up tale, a true story, a 'how to' book.
Plan pages with quick sketches.
Draw and write or dictate the words.
Add a title, author's name and 'about the author' page.

activities.title: Readers' Theatre
materials: A short, familiar story with repeated lines
Picture cue cards for each part
steps: Read the story together a few times.
Children choose parts; non-readers use picture cue cards or echo lines.
Practise voices that show feelings.
Perform for another group or for families.

activities.title: Outdoor Story Walk
materials: Pages of a picture book in plastic sleeves
Tape or clips for a fence
steps: Post story pages along a fence or path in order.
Walk from page to page, reading together.
At each stop, invite a movement (hop like the rabbit, tiptoe like the mouse).
Ask children to predict what happens next before each page.
activities.safety: Sunscreen and hats in sun, layers in cold; keep the route inside the yard or a supervised path.

activities.title: Tell It Again Chair
materials: Folk tales and picture books from many cultures
steps: Read or tell a short folk tale.
Invite volunteers to retell it from the storyteller chair.
Encourage changes: a new ending, a different animal, a twist.
Compare: 'How was your version different?'

activities.title: Chalk Story Trail
steps: Draw a winding trail of story scenes on pavement together.
Children hop, skip or balance from scene to scene.
At each scene, someone adds a sentence to the story.
Change the trail and tell a new story.
activities.safety: Use a traffic-free area; sun protection and water on warm days.

activities.title: Sound Effects Band
materials: Paper to crinkle, pots and wooden spoons
A short story with lots of action
steps: Read the story once.
Brainstorm sounds for rain, footsteps, doors and wind.
Assign each child a sound and a cue word.
Read again while the band adds sound effects.

activities.title: Character Freeze-Frames
steps: Children move around the space to the music.
When it stops, call a character and feeling ('a grumpy giant').
Everyone freezes in a shape that shows it.
Invite children to guess each other's characters.

activities.title: Book Launch Party
steps: Set up an author table for each child who wants one.
Children read or show their books to visitors or another group.
Add books to the reading corner for borrowing.
Celebrate every author with applause.

activities.title: Family Story Interviews
steps: Practise interview questions together: 'What did you play when you were little?'
Children interview each other first.
Send the question card home for an optional family interview.
Children share family stories by drawing or telling.

activities.title: Wordless Book Narrators
steps: Look at the pictures together without reading.
Invite pairs to take turns telling what happens on each page.
Add sticky-note words or symbols for favourite pages.
Compare how different pairs told the same book.

schedule.focus: Telling stories out loud and stories from home
Characters come alive with puppets, sound and drama
Writing, drawing and sharing our own books

observe: Does a child's story have a clear beginning, middle and end?
What new words or story phrases ('once upon a time', 'suddenly') show up in play?
How does a child build on a friend's idea in a shared story?
Who takes the stage readily, and who prefers to help backstage — how can each be supported?
How does a child use pictures, letters and symbols to carry meaning?
What family or cultural stories do children bring in?
family: Send home the family interview card as an optional, any-language activity.
Invite family members to tell or read a story, in person or by a recorded audio clip.
Ask families to save clean single socks and fabric scraps for puppets.
Share a 'tell me a story about…' prompt for the drive or walk home.
Invite families to the Book Launch Party or send photos of finished books home.
inclusion: Offer picture cue cards, echo lines or a recorded line so every child can join readers' theatre.
Accept stories told through gesture, sign, drawing, puppets or a communication device.
Provide pencil grips, thicker markers and pre-drawn panels for children who find drawing tiring.
Give a quieter corner or small audience for children who feel nervous performing.
Allow extra processing time during circle stories; no one is rushed or put on the spot.
Talk with families and any resource consultant about communication supports used at home.

tips: Open French story time with 'Il était une fois…' and invite children to chime in.
Make some class books bilingual, with English and French on each page.
Invite families to tell a story in their home language; children can act it out.
Accept story contributions in any language and celebrate mixing languages.

safety_notes: In mixed-age groups, keep story stones and small craft pieces away from children under 3.
Educators handle staplers and hole punches; use non-toxic, washable art materials.
Outdoor story activities: sun protection, weather-appropriate clothing and a traffic-free space.

title: Summer Camp: Outdoor Adventures
summary: Four weeks of camp-style fun: active games, nature scavenger hunts, water play, camp songs and traditions. Children build friendships, independence and outdoor confidence while learning to keep themselves safe in the sun and heat.
big_questions: What makes a great day at camp?
How do we keep our bodies safe and cool in the summer sun?
What can we discover when we explore outside?

goals.text: Children enjoy vigorous outdoor play and build strength, speed and coordination.
Children take growing responsibility for sun safety, water breaks and rest in the shade.
Children explore, collect clues and solve problems in nature.
Children feel part of a camp community with shared songs, names and traditions.
Children play fairly, include others and cheer each other on.

activities.title: Camp Name and Flag
steps: Brainstorm and vote on a camp or group name.
Design a flag with handprints, symbols and the name.
Invite every child to add their mark.
Raise the flag at the opening circle each morning.

activities.title: Nature Scavenger Hunt
materials: Picture checklists (something rough, a feather on the ground — look only, a Y-shaped stick, three colours of leaves)
Clipboards or egg cartons for found treasures
steps: Hand out picture checklists to pairs or small teams.
Teams search and tick off finds, collecting only fallen items.
Gather to compare treasures and unusual finds.
Return natural items to where they belong.
activities.safety: Sunscreen, hats and water bottles. Look-only for feathers, bugs and mushrooms; never pick or eat berries or plants found outside. Head count before and after.

activities.title: Sprinkler Obstacle Course
steps: Set up a course on grass that weaves through the sprinkler.
Children crawl, hop and dash through stations.
Invite children to redesign the course.
End with a cool-down in the shade.
activities.safety: Water play only, on grass (not pavement); an educator stays within arm's reach of the water area. Walking feet near wet edges; sunscreen reapplied after. Turn off the water and tip out containers when done.

activities.title: Bucket Brigade Relay
steps: Form teams in lines between a full tub and an empty one.
Pass water by cup or sponge down the line.
Measure how much water each team moved together.
Talk about how teamwork made it easier.
activities.safety: An educator stays within arm's reach of the tubs and buckets; tip out all water when done. Play on grass; offer shade and drinking water breaks.

activities.title: Shadow Detectives
steps: In the morning, trace each other's shadows with chalk.
Trace again at lunchtime and compare lengths.
Ask, 'When is the sun strongest? Where is the shade?'
Make a map of shady spots in the yard.
activities.safety: Keep tracing short in full sun; hats and sunscreen on; never look directly at the sun.

activities.title: Sun Safety Squad
materials: Sun safety picture checklist (hat, sunscreen, shade, water)
steps: Talk about how sun and heat can affect our bodies.
Practise putting on sunscreen with an educator's help, checking ears, neck and noses.
Make 'squad badges' for checking the list before going outside.
Squad leaders remind the group at water breaks.
activities.safety: Use only each child's own or family-approved sunscreen; check for skin sensitivities and allergies.

activities.title: Campfire Song Circle
steps: Gather around the pretend fire.
Sing call-and-response camp songs and echo chants.
Invite children to add verses or actions.
Ask families for songs from home to add to the camp songbook.

activities.title: Parachute and Team Games
steps: Warm up with parachute waves and 'mushroom'.
Play cooperative games: bouncing balls, cat and mouse, colour swap.
Invite children to invent a new parachute game.
Cool down in the shade with water.
activities.safety: Shady area or cooler times of day; water breaks every 15–20 minutes; move indoors in extreme heat.

activities.title: Nature Art Mandalas
materials: Fallen leaves, petals, sticks and pine cones
A hoop or chalk circle on the ground
steps: Collect fallen natural materials only.
Arrange them in circles and patterns inside the hoop.
Photograph the finished art.
Leave it for nature or return materials to the ground.
activities.safety: Fallen materials only; no picking plants, berries or mushrooms; wash hands after. Sun protection on.

activities.title: Water Table Boat Builders
materials: Foil, corks, foam trays and craft sticks
Toy figures or wooden blocks as 'passengers'
steps: Invite children to build a boat that floats.
Test it in the water table.
Add passengers one at a time and count before it sinks.
Redesign and test again.
activities.safety: An educator stays within arm's reach of the water table; tip out water when done. In mixed-age groups, keep corks and small parts from under-3s.

activities.title: Bug Hotel Build
materials: Hollow stems, pine cones, bark and straw
steps: Talk about where small creatures rest and hide.
Fill the crate with natural materials in layers.
Place it in a quiet, shady spot.
Check daily with bug viewers and record visitors.
activities.safety: Gloves for gathering; observe insects without rough handling; wash hands after. Watch for bees and wasps and move away calmly.

activities.title: Cloud Watching and Sky Journals
steps: Lie on blankets in the shade and look up.
Name shapes you see in the clouds.
Draw a cloud and write or tell what it became.
Notice how the sky changes during the week.
activities.safety: Shade only; never look directly at the sun; hats and water nearby.

activities.title: Camp Fruit Salad
materials: Washed fruit (berries, melon, grapes, soft peaches)
steps: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first.
Wash hands together.
Children cut soft fruit with child-safe knives while an educator handles tough cuts.
Serve and talk about favourite summer fruits from home.
activities.safety: Check every child's allergy and dietary list first; no nuts; offer alternatives. Grapes cut in quarters lengthwise and berries halved for younger children. Children sit to eat; keep food in the shade.

activities.title: Sponge Toss Targets
materials: Chalk targets on a wall or fence
steps: Soak sponges and throw at chalk targets.
Score points for hitting each ring.
Move the throwing line back for a challenge.
Count how many targets the group washed away.
activities.safety: An educator stays within arm's reach of the buckets; tip out water when done. Aim at targets, not faces.

activities.title: Treasure Map Quest
materials: A 'treasure' box with a group surprise (stickers, a new game)
steps: Show the yard map and find landmarks together.
Teams follow clues from spot to spot.
Invite children to draw their own maps and hide clues for others.
Open the treasure together at the end.
activities.safety: Stay within the fenced yard or a supervised area; sun protection and water breaks.

activities.title: Camp Talent Campfire
steps: Invite children to sign up to share a song, joke, dance, trick or drawing.
Hold the show around the pretend campfire.
Clap and cheer for everyone, performers and audience.
Close with the camp song and a memory share.

activities.title: Ice Excavation
materials: Large ice blocks with toy animals frozen inside
steps: Set ice blocks on trays in the shade.
Children rescue the animals using warm water, salt and tools.
Compare which method melts ice fastest.
Talk about how cold water feels on hot hands.
activities.safety: An educator stays within arm's reach of the water and trays; tip out water when done. Salt can sting cuts; rinse hands after. Frozen toys must be larger than a child's fist.

activities.title: Kindness Camp Badges
steps: Talk about how campers look out for each other.
Invite children to notice a friend being kind and add it to the jar.
Read shout-outs at circle.
Children make a badge for the friend they noticed.

activities.title: Rainy Day Fort Builders
steps: On a rainy or extreme-heat day, invite teams to build a fort indoors.
Plan where doors and windows go.
Read, sing or tell stories inside the forts.
Tidy up together and vote on next time's design.
activities.safety: Check flashlights have screwed-shut battery doors; keep forts low and away from shelves that could tip.

schedule.focus: Welcome to camp: our name, songs and first explorations
Water and sun: staying cool, safe and playful
Wild explorers: bugs, maps and nature art
Camp traditions: kindness, favourites and a closing campfire

observe: Who remembers hats, sunscreen and water on their own, and who still needs a reminder?
How do children include a new or quieter camper in games?
How does a child respond when a team game doesn't go their way?
Which nature finds spark the most questions?
How does a child plan and change a boat or obstacle course design after testing?
Which songs and traditions do children bring into their own play?
Does any child show signs of heat stress (flushed, tired, cranky) that call for shade and water?
family: Share a daily camp checklist: labelled water bottle, hat, sunscreen, clothes that can get wet, a change of clothes.
Invite families to send a favourite song, game or summer memory from their childhood or culture.
Send home the scavenger hunt picture list to try at a local park.
Share photos from the week and the camp song so families can sing along.
Invite families to the closing Talent Campfire or share a recording of it.
inclusion: Offer a picture schedule of the camp day and give a heads-up before transitions.
Choose accessible routes and stations for children using mobility aids; adapt games so everyone can play seated or standing.
Provide a shady, quiet 'base camp' for children who need a sensory break.
Offer alternatives to getting wet (water table, sponge toss from the side) for children who dislike water play.
Use buddies, first/then language and extra processing time during busy group games.
Talk with families and any resource consultant about heat sensitivities, medications or supports.

tips: Teach a short French camp chant or sing a familiar song in French at circle.
Make the sun-safety checklist bilingual: 'chapeau, crème solaire, ombre, eau'.
Invite families to share camp or summer songs in their home languages.
Accept answers and clues in any language during games and hunts.

safety_notes: Heat and sun: sunscreen and hats, shade, water breaks every 15–20 minutes, active play at cooler times, and move indoors in extreme heat or humidex alerts.
Water play only — no swimming or wading activities in this unit. An educator stays within arm's reach of every water station; tip out all water when done.
Food: check every child's allergy and dietary list first, no nuts, wash hands, cut food to size for younger children.
Outdoors: look-only for wildlife, never pick or eat berries, mushrooms or plants; keep head counts at every transition.

title: Kindness and Community Changemakers
summary: Children explore empathy and fairness, then choose and carry out a real helping project for their centre, neighbourhood or environment. Seeing that their ideas and actions make a difference builds belonging, confidence and care for others.
big_questions: How can we tell what someone else is feeling?
What does 'fair' mean — is it always the same for everyone?
What can kids do to make our community better?

goals.text: Children notice and name kind actions and how they make others feel.
Children talk about fairness and solve everyday conflicts with growing independence.
Children plan and carry out a group helping project from idea to finish.
Children care for shared spaces and the natural environment.
continuum: Social: respect for others and the environment

goals.text: Children express gratitude and ideas through words, art and action.

activities.title: Kindness Detectives
steps: Talk about what kindness looks like and sounds like.
Children wear detective badges and watch for kind acts during play.
Record each one with a drawing or words on a sticky note.
Read the board at circle and notice how kindness spreads.

activities.title: Fair or Not Fair?
materials: Scenario picture cards (sharing snacks, taking turns, a friend who needs a step stool)
steps: Show a scenario and ask, 'Is this fair? Why?'
Invite children to vote and explain their thinking.
Talk about how fair sometimes means everyone gets what they need, not the same thing.
List ideas for making things fair in our room.

activities.title: In Their Shoes Story Time
materials: Picture books showing many families, abilities and cultures
A pair of 'perspective' shoes or slippers
steps: Read a story where a character has a problem or big feeling.
Pause and ask, 'How do you think they feel? How do you know?'
Invite a child to 'step into the shoes' and speak as the character.
Brainstorm ways someone could help.

activities.title: Litter Patrol
steps: Walk the yard or a nearby park with gloves and grabbers.
Pick up paper and wrappers with grabbers, sorting trash and recycling.
Tally what you found and talk about where it came from.
Wash hands well when you return.
activities.safety: Gloves and grabbers only. Never touch glass, needles, sharp metal, animal waste or anything unknown — stop and call an educator. Sun protection and weather-appropriate clothing.

activities.title: Community Thank-You Cards
steps: List people who help our centre and neighbourhood (cooks, cleaners, crossing guards, librarians).
Invite each child to choose someone to thank.
Draw and write or dictate a message.
Deliver cards in person or by mail as a group.

activities.title: Everybody Wins Games
steps: Play cooperative games where no one is out: shrinking hoops, group ball keep-up, parachute challenges.
Pause to ask, 'How did we help each other?'
Invite children to change a rule so more people can join in.
Celebrate the group's teamwork.
activities.safety: Clear, flat space; water breaks; sun protection or warm layers as the weather calls for.

activities.title: Changemaker Project Vote
steps: Brainstorm helping ideas: planting for pollinators, a book swap, fixing toys, cards for a seniors' home.
Children explain why their idea matters.
Vote with stickers and choose one or two projects.
Make a simple picture plan of who does what.

activities.title: Pollinator Planting
steps: Talk about bees and butterflies and why they need flowers.
Fill pots, plant seeds or seedlings and label them.
Make a watering rota with names and pictures.
Check growth and visitors each day.
activities.safety: Choose plants known to be non-toxic; gloves for children with sensitive skin; wash hands after soil play. Observe bees calmly from a distance.

activities.title: Gratitude Chain
steps: Invite children to draw or write something or someone they are thankful for.
Link the strips into a chain.
Add new links each day of the unit.
Measure how long the chain grows and hang it for families to see.

activities.title: Toy and Book Repair Shop
materials: Worn books and broken toys from the centre
steps: Collect items that need care and write repair tickets.
Children decide what each item needs: tape, cleaning or gluing.
Work in pairs to fix and test each item.
Return fixed items to shelves or a book swap.
activities.safety: Educators check items first and set aside anything sharp or with batteries. Use non-toxic glue and child-safe cleaning wipes.

activities.title: What Could I Say? Role-Play
materials: Simple prompt cards ('Can I play?', 'I didn't like that', 'Are you okay?')
steps: Act out a tricky moment with puppets: someone is left out or a toy is grabbed.
Ask, 'What could they say or do?'
Invite pairs to try the scene with a kind or fair ending.
Post the best phrases where children can see them.

schedule.focus: What kindness, empathy and fairness look like
Changemakers in action: choosing and doing a helping project

observe: Which kind acts does a child notice in others — and in themselves?
How does a child explain why something is or isn't fair?
What does a child do when a friend is upset?
How do children share jobs and decisions during the helping project?
Who uses the 'What could I say?' phrases in real moments?
How does a child talk about caring for plants, animals or the yard?
family: Share the Kindness Spotted board and invite families to add kind acts from home.
Invite families to suggest community helpers or places the group could thank.
If the project is a collection or book swap, make giving fully optional and private — never single out who brought what.
Share a family 'gratitude at dinner' or 'kindness at bedtime' idea.
Invite families to share how kindness or helping is practised in their culture or community.
inclusion: Use picture scenario cards and feelings visuals so all children can join discussions.
Offer several ways to vote and contribute: stickers, pointing, sign, drawing or words.
Give every child a meaningful project job that matches their strengths and comfort.
Adapt cooperative games so children using mobility aids or who need a slower pace fully take part.
Allow extra processing time and a quieter role-play space for children who find groups overwhelming.
Talk with families and any resource consultant about social goals and supports that help at home.

tips: Teach friendly phrases in French: 'Veux-tu jouer?', 'Ça va?', 'Merci!'
Label the Kindness Spotted board and gratitude chain in English and French.
Invite families to add 'thank you' and 'friend' in their home languages to the chain.
Accept ideas in any language during votes and discussions.

safety_notes: Litter Patrol: gloves and grabbers only; children never touch glass, needles, sharp items or waste — they call an educator.
Gardening: non-toxic plants, wash hands after soil, observe bees and insects calmly.
Keep any donation or collection project optional and private so no family feels pressure.
Check repaired items for sharp edges and batteries before they go back into play.
